Jeffrey Katzenberg Is Starting an AI Animation Studio and Says Talent Is the Hard Part
Katzenberg told TheWrap he will launch a platform or studio making animated features and TV with AI tools, partnering with filmmakers, days after posting a manifesto urging Hollywood to embrace AI.
Jeffrey Katzenberg, who ran Disney animation through "The Little Mermaid" and "The Lion King," plans a new company making animated films and television with generative AI, either as a digital platform or a studio. He said AI output was "slop" until the last few months and now marks "a real transformative moment." His stated plan is to partner "talented filmmakers and AI" and to start at the top of the market before moving to consumer tools. Asked what could stop him, after Quibi burned through $1.75 billion, he named one thing: talent. No financing, partners or launch date were disclosed.
Potential Talent Implication: Katzenberg says talent is the one thing his AI animation studio cannot get cheaply, which makes equity in the company the term that matters for the directors he recruits.
The Facts
  • Katzenberg spoke to TheWrap's Sharon Waxman (WaxWord) after posting a manifesto on X earlier in the week urging Hollywood to embrace AI.
  • Plan: "either a digital platform or an actual studio" to create animated entertainment using AI; animated feature films and television "with the best talent and the most aspirational content."
  • Quote: "Partner with talented filmmakers and AI to deliver the resources of the AI world and to marry that with best talent."
  • Quote on barriers: "That's the hard part," referring to talent.
  • Quote: "If barriers and cost come down, more films will get made, there will be more jobs, new forms of storytelling will emerge."
  • Background in the story: Quibi launched in 2020 with $1.75 billion in capital and shut in about six months; Katzenberg partnered with Kimbal Musk last year on drone entertainment.
  • On Disney: "Pixar could never have been created inside Disney animation," he said, adding that Roy Disney asked him not to make "Toy Story."
  • Same week: Katzenberg discussed the essay on The Town with Matthew Belloni and Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw (episode "Jeffrey Katzenberg on Why Hollywood Must Embrace AI").
  • No financing, partners, name or timeline disclosed ("Stay tuned for details").
· TheWrap · Sharon Waxman · 2026-09-25 · https://www.thewrap.com/industry-news/business/jeffrey-katzenberg-ai-animation-studio/ · Provenance: named-exec-quote source ↗
Puck Sold a Majority Stake to RedBird at $250 Million, and Staff Stock Gets Paid Out
RedBird, the Paramount co-control owner, is taking a majority stake in five-year-old Puck; Standard Investments and TPG exit, and employees with vested stock or options get cash plus continued ownership.
RedBird Capital Partners signed a deal to become Puck's lead investor at about a $250 million valuation, according to a staff memo from CEO Sarah Personette and co-founder Jon Kelly obtained by Variety. Founding backers Standard Investments and TPG exit; RIT Capital stays as a minority investor. The memo says employees with vested stock or options receive "a combination of liquidity and continued ownership," and a new equity incentive plan follows at closing, expected in about a month pending regulatory approval. RedBird's Gerry Cardinale sits on the Paramount board, a company Puck covers.
Potential Talent Implication: Puck's writers built a $250 million company in five years, and the ones holding vested stock or options now get paid in cash and keep a stake.
The Facts
  • Buyer: RedBird Capital Partners, managing partner Gerry Cardinale, a Paramount director and "co-control owner" of Paramount (Variety).
  • Valuation: approximately $250 million, per the memo.
  • Exiting: Standard Investments and TPG, backers since inception. Remaining: RIT Capital, minority.
  • Employees: vested stock or options holders get "a combination of liquidity and continued ownership in the company"; a new equity incentive plan will be detailed at closing.
  • Closing: about one month, subject to regulatory approval.
  • Stated uses: invest in Puck and Air Mail, hire talent, enter new markets, pursue acquisitions, expand "our IP into new formats and channels."
  • Memo: the deal "does not change our editorial independence."
  • RedBird's other holdings named by Variety: Paramount Skydance, Artists Equity (Ben Affleck and Matt Damon), Ari Emanuel's Mari, Fenway Sports Group; RedBird IMI owns 50% of Banijay.
  • THR separately reported the deal as RedBird becoming "lead investor."

Netflix Signed Alec Berg to an Overall Deal With a Series Already Set

Disney's Legal Chief Told Staff His Department Will Be Much Smaller and Partly Automated
Horacio Gutierrez's Sept. 18 memo to Disney's legal and global affairs group names automation, self-service, alternative legal providers and outsourcing as replacements, with wider Disney layoffs expected as soon as next week.
Disney's chief legal and global affairs officer, Horacio Gutierrez, told his department of fewer than 1,000 people that it "will be a much smaller organization than it is today," in a memo Deadline obtained. He listed the new models: "automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies," self-service, "alternative legal providers," shared services and outsourcing. The memo went out the same day Disney named former Character.AI chief executive Karandeep Anand its first chief technology officer. Deadline reports broader company layoffs are expected to begin as early as next week, after cuts in April and July. Disney declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney's legal department, which papers talent deals, is moving work to automation and outside legal providers, so the business-affairs counterpart on a Disney deal could be fewer people working from more standardized terms.
The Facts
  • Memo date: noon, Sept. 18, to the Legal and Global Affairs (LGA) department, fewer than 1,000 members globally (Deadline, exclusive).
  • Quote: "LGA will be a much smaller organization than it is today, and some of you will personally be affected by decisions we make in this process."
  • Quote: "we'll have to consider a whole range of new models for different workloads, including automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies, moving to self-service models where appropriate, engaging alternative legal providers and others, and new expanded share services, even outsourcing."
  • Deadline: unspecified LGA cuts are separate from the next company round, which is expected to begin as early as next week.
  • Same day: Disney named Karandeep Anand, former Character.AI CEO, its first CTO, reporting to CEO Josh D'Amaro.
  • Prior Disney cuts: April and July 2026; a voluntary early-retirement offer was announced in August by Chief People Officer Sonia Coleman.
  • Gutierrez joined from Spotify in late 2021, replacing Alan Braverman.
  • Disney declined to comment on the memo or on the timing and scope of cuts.

Apple TV Won 28 Emmys and Still Has to Prove It Makes Money
Apple has raised Apple TV's price four times since 2022, to $15 a month, and churn has held near 5 percent, but Apple discloses no subscriber or TV revenue figures.
Julia Alexander asks whether new Apple CEO John Ternus will keep funding Apple TV after its record 28 Emmys. Apple has never broken out subscribers or TV revenue; Eddy Cue told Puck's Matt Belloni last October that global subscribers were "significantly more than" analyst estimates of 40 million to 45 million. Luminate estimated Apple's share of U.S. original streaming viewing at about 6.5 percent in the first half. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman told Puck that Ternus will follow Cue, who will recommend continued heavy investment "even though they're losing money on it."
Potential Talent Implication: Apple keeps paying for awards-level television while its streaming business has no disclosed profit, and that spending holds as long as Eddy Cue backs it, which makes Cue's standing inside Apple part of the risk on any Apple deal.
The Facts
  • Emmys: 28 wins this month, Apple's most ever; about 90 over six years (Puck).
  • John Ternus was promoted to Apple CEO about two weeks before the Emmys.
  • Pricing: four increases between July 2022 and July 2026; now $15 a month, three times the 2019 launch price.
  • Churn: steady around 5 percent (industry average) since August 2025 (Puck, citing data).
  • Subscribers: never disclosed. Cue: "significantly more than" 40 million to 45 million globally (October 2025). Ampere: just over 18.5 million U.S. as of Q1.
  • Viewing: Apple has never appeared on Nielsen's monthly Gauge (under 1 percent of U.S. connected-TV viewing). Luminate: about 6.5 percent of U.S. original streaming viewing, first half 2026.
  • Services revenue: up 12 percent year over year to more than $30.7 billion in the latest quarter.
  • Ads: Cue to Screen International last November: no plans for ads, but not saying "no forever." Antenna: ad tiers were 78 percent of new U.S. subscriptions over nine quarters.
  • Gurman quote: Ternus is "going to do what Eddy recommends," and Cue will recommend continued heavy investment "even though they're losing money on it."
  • Cue recently took over the App Store in addition to services (Puck).

The Travers Estate Can Make a Mary Poppins Series Without Disney
Tom Winchester optioned the rights to P.L. Travers' eight novels from her estate's trustees; Deadline reports the series does not need Disney's buy-in and talks with Disney are very early.
Tom Winchester of Pure Fiction Television, the independent backed by See-Saw Films and UK agency Hamilton Hodell, has optioned the Mary Poppins rights from the trustees of P.L. Travers' estate and is developing a live-action series, Deadline reported in its Dish column, which relies on unnamed sourcing. The series goes back to Travers' eight books, and Disney's 1964 film is not its source. Per the report, the project does not need Disney's buy-in on rights; very early conversations with Disney are taking place and nothing is agreed. Winchester is approaching showrunners, and the project is at pitch stage.
Potential Talent Implication: The Travers trustees still control the book rights after two Disney films, so the estate is choosing the producer, the format and whether Disney, which made Mary Poppins famous, gets in at all.
The Facts
  • Developer/producer: Tom Winchester, Pure Fiction Television (backed by See-Saw Films, producer of Slow Horses and Heartstopper, and UK talent agency Hamilton Hodell).
  • Rights: optioned from the trustees of the P.L. Travers estate; developed "on behalf of" the trustees.
  • Source material: Travers' original eight Mary Poppins books; described as more "mysterious, mercurial and dangerous" than the film version.
  • Disney: "very early-stage conversations"; the project "doesn't need Disney's buy-in from a rights perspective"; "Nothing has been agreed." Pure Fiction and Disney declined to comment.
  • Status: pitch stage; Winchester approaching "top level showrunners."
  • Prior Disney adaptations: Mary Poppins (1964, Julie Andrews, Dick Van Dyke); Mary Poppins Returns (2018, Emily Blunt, Lin-Manuel Miranda, dir. Rob Marshall).

Rob Minkoff Is in Talks to Lead Particle 6's AI-Assisted Feature
Storm Dogs, a family film about a toddler and a pack of dogs, would build both from live-action performances and AI, with production targeted for 2027.
Rob Minkoff, co-director of The Lion King and director of Stuart Little, is in advanced discussions to be creative lead on Storm Dogs, the next film from Particle 6, the London company behind the AI performer Tilly Norwood, Variety reported. He would develop the story, characters and script with the company's van der Velden. Particle 6 said actors' expressions, physicality and inflections will be applied to photorealistic animated characters, not just their voices. A spokesperson said AI means "neither toddlers nor animals need to be on set for long hours." Production targets 2027.
Potential Talent Implication: Particle 6 is applying actors' expressions and physicality to AI-built characters, so for a performer on Storm Dogs the term that carries the value is who can reuse that captured performance, and where.
The Facts
  • Project: Storm Dogs, family comedy-drama; toddler Poppy is separated from her caretaker by a storm in an English village and is guided home by dogs.
  • Minkoff: in "advanced discussions" to serve as creative lead; co-director of The Lion King, director of Stuart Little.
  • Method (per Particle 6): "live-action performances with photorealistic animated characters," a mix of AI tools, traditional approaches and human actors; the actor's "expressions, physicality and inflections are applied to the animated characters, rather than just using their voice." The toddler and dogs are "created" with a mix of live-action performance and AI.
  • Spokesperson: AI is "a real bonus" because "neither toddlers nor animals need to be on set for long hours."
  • van der Velden: "I'm not interested in AI as a replacement for human creativity"; "keeping every creative decision in human hands."
  • Minkoff: Particle 6 is "serious about exploring how new production methods can expand how filmmakers' imaginations are realized on screen."
  • Timing: in development, targeting a 2027 production start.
  • Context: Particle 6's Tilly Norwood stars in its first feature, Misaligned, which began production this month.

2026-09-24 Thursday 12 stories

The Federal Film Credit Bill Counts Star Salaries Toward the 20 Percent
Sens. Tim Scott and Adam Schiff and four House members introduced a 20% federal credit on U.S. production compensation Thursday, above-the-line salaries included, with 5% uplifts that can reach 30%.
A bipartisan group introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act on Thursday. It pays a 20% credit on compensation tied to a production, excluding residuals, and TheWrap reports that above-the-line salaries count, as they do in the UK and Canada. Uplifts of 5% each, to a 30% ceiling, go to shoots in rural opportunity zones or federal disaster areas (Los Angeles County qualifies until 2030), independent productions, shoots across 10 or more states, and studios that raise domestic output. Credits stack on state incentives. Congress is out until after the midterms; Schiff is aiming for the lame-duck session.
Potential Talent Implication: If the bill passes, a producer earns back 20 percent of star and director salaries, and up to 30 percent on an independent shot in Los Angeles, the same above-the-line credit that sent Barbie and Deadpool & Wolverine to shoot abroad.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, introduced Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.
  • Co-sponsors: Sens. Tim Scott (R-SC), Adam Schiff (D-CA); Reps. Linda Sanchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), Laura Friedman (D-CA). Other backers: Reps. Judy Chu, David Kustoff, Mike Carey, Tom Suozzi.
  • Base rate: 20% of compensation directly related to a production, excluding residuals (Deadline). TheWrap: above-the-line talent salaries count toward the base.
  • Uplifts (5% each, 30% maximum, per TheWrap): at least 30% of principal photography days in a rural qualified opportunity zone or federally declared disaster area; independent production; at least 50% of principal photography and $10M in qualified compensation across 10 or more states; studio increases domestic productions relative to a historical foreign base amount.
  • L.A. County was declared a federal disaster area in 2025 after the Palisades and Altadena fires and keeps the designation until 2030 (TheWrap).
  • Eligibility: total cost above $1M; 75% of production in the U.S.; post-production and VFX covered; animation covered (TheWrap). Excluded: news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising, corporate video.
  • Credits transferable; stack on top of state incentives (31 states have them, per TheWrap).
  • Timing: House in recess through the midterms; Schiff said the plan is to pass it in the lame-duck session, possibly attached to a major funding bill. TheWrap: bill would take effect for productions at the start of 2027.
  • TheWrap: the $1M floor excludes microbudget films like Obsession (reported $750,000 budget, more than $500M global).
  • MPA statement: passage "could inject $250 billion into the country's economy and deliver nearly 145,000 new jobs every year."
  • Christopher Nolan (DGA president): "the most significant legislative effort in a generation to promote domestic film and television production."
  • Schiff credited Trump for the momentum and said he worked with the White House, Jon Voight and Spencer Pratt.

Sony Paid for a S.W.A.T. Spinoff Itself and Renewed It Before Starz Did
Sony ordered 10 episodes of S.W.A.T. Exiles with no buyer attached in May 2025, found Starz more than a year later, and has already ordered season two on its own money.
Sony Pictures Television self-financed S.W.A.T. Exiles, the Shemar Moore spinoff, as sole producer and distributor after CBS ended the original in May 2025, TV president Katherine Pope told TheWrap. Shopping it first would have cost the stages and the crew, so Sony greenlit 10 episodes days after the finale and sold it to Starz over a year later. Sony has renewed a second season without a Starz commitment; Starz will decide on its own season two based on new subscribers and engagement. Pope said the model only works on a show "produced at a number," not a $15 million-an-episode series.
Potential Talent Implication: When the studio fronts the money itself, a star and crew keep working instead of waiting years for a buyer, but only on a show made at a fixed number, with the platform's terms set after the risk is taken.
The Facts
  • Original: S.W.A.T. ran eight seasons on CBS, co-produced by Sony Pictures TV and CBS Studios; CBS reversed cancellations after seasons 6 and 7; the finale aired May 2025.
  • CBS passed on the spinoff because it had newer franchises in development (Pope).
  • Sony gave S.W.A.T. Exiles a 10-episode order in May 2025, days after the finale, as sole producer and distributor, keeping the Los Angeles sets and crew.
  • Showrunner: Jason Ning, under an overall deal with Sony. Executive producer Neal Moritz.
  • Distributor: Starz, landed "over a year after Sony's green light." Premieres Friday, September 25, 2026.
  • Sony renewed season two without Starz's commitment. Starz president Alison Hoffman: a season-two decision rests on the show's ability to "attract new subscribers, deepen engagement among existing viewers."
  • Pope: "The No. 1 thing about this model is it has to be able to be produced at a number... It's a big number. It's a lot of risk, but... it's not $15 million dollars an episode."
  • Pope: "TV used to be very much a deficit business and a risk-based business, and we got to... streaming deals where you didn't have to take on risk."
  • Pope said the per-season production number stayed essentially the same season after season.

Paramount's Four-Indie-Films Pledge Counts Any Original Screenplay
The combined company targets $6 billion in annual savings within three years and carries about $80 billion in debt. A missed theatrical target costs $30 million per film.
Paramount's settlement with 12 states requires at least four independent films a year, but the consent decree defines an independent film as any movie based on an original screenplay or simply co-produced by Paramount, TheWrap reported in an analysis Wednesday. The Warner Bros. Discovery deal, expected to close in about two weeks, also requires 30 theatrical films a year for two years and 32 for the three after, with a $30 million penalty per missed film. Experts quoted called the penalties toothless. Paramount already holds overall deals with Jon M. Chu, the Duffer Brothers and James Mangold.
Potential Talent Implication: An original script Paramount co-produces satisfies the independent-film quota, which leaves outside independent producers with no protected slot; the 30-film theatrical floor is the term that actually guarantees buying.
The Facts
  • Output terms: at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years, 32 a year for the next three; at least four a year must be independent films; at least 20% must be blockbusters.
  • Definition: the consent decree defines independent films as movies "based on an original screenplay" or simply co-produced by Paramount (TheWrap's reading).
  • Penalties: $30 million per film that misses the theatrical goal; forced divestiture of the 49% Miramax stake within 12 months, and of BET, Comedy Central, VH1, Smithsonian, Destination America and Science Channel within 120 days, for other breaches.

The Paramount Settlement Fixes a 45-Day Theatrical Window for Five Years
Thirty films a year for two years, then 32, at least four of them independent, and $30 million per missed film goes into the Hollywood guilds' health and retirement plans.
Paramount Skydance settled the antitrust suit brought by 12 state attorneys general on Monday, clearing the last obstacle to its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery. The proposed consent decree runs five years and, alongside the release commitments, guarantees a 45-day theatrical window with no streaming release before 90 days. No divestiture is required to close. Antitrust expert Matt Stoller told The Ankler that half the films need only be co-produced. Jane Fonda, reading the agreement, said a force majeure clause voids its terms in a strike, labor disruption or recession.
Potential Talent Implication: Paramount now owes a 45-day theatrical window for five years, which gives release bonuses, first-cycle backend and every term defined by a theatrical run a fixed number to point at instead of a negotiation.
The Facts
  • The suit was brought by 12 state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, against Paramount Skydance's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Settlement announced Monday, September 21, at a Bonta press conference.
  • Film commitments, quoting the proposed consent decree via THR: minimum 30 films per year for the first two years, rising to 32 per year for the following three. At least 20 (later 21) must be wide releases. At least four must be independent films. At least 20 percent must carry budgets over $50 million.
  • Windowing: a guaranteed 45-day theatrical window, with no SVOD window until at least 90 days.
  • Production spend: at least $300 million more annually on U.S. film production than was spent in 2025, or $1.5 billion across the agreement. Plus commitments on pricing to theaters.
  • Breach remedies on the film commitment: forced divestiture of Paramount's stake in Miramax, and $30 million per film short contributed to the healthcare and retirement plans of the major Hollywood guilds.
  • Lots: the combined entity may not sell or close the Paramount or Warner Bros. lots during the commitment period, and must use commercially reasonable efforts to operate them consistent with past practice, including leasing to third parties.
  • Cable: separate negotiation of basic cable carriage for five years, restrictions on affiliate fee changes, and a bar on using one defendant's confidential information in the other's affiliate negotiations. No cable divestitures required; a court can order divestiture on breach.
  • News: a five-member News Editorial Independence Board, named by Paramount's board of directors, each member a journalist of at least ten years' practice, with no more than two affiliated with the same political party.
  • Matt Stoller, to The Ankler: "Half of those have to be at least co-produced by Warnermount. So they don't have to make more than 15 or 16 films, and even those, they could just co-produce them. So the actual commitment is fewer films than they make now, for both studios combined."
  • Stoller on the force majeure provision: it includes an economic recession or labor strikes, so "if they do something that causes a strike or labor disruption of some sort, it says here that's beyond their control."
  • Jane Fonda, in a statement reported by TheWrap: the settlement "has a 'Force Majeure' clause stating that all its terms are void if there is a strike, labor disruptions, or an economic recession, meaning this settlement is also a union-buster."
  • Per Puck: Ellison met privately with New York AG Letitia James in Los Angeles on Friday, then met Bonta in the Bay Area; Bonta would not sign off unless the major Hollywood unions were on board, and Ellison spent the weekend calling guild heads.
  • Connecticut AG William Tong: "Connecticut wanted and demanded full divestiture of CNN and CBS News... I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more."
  • The Writers Guild of America settled its own suit blocking the merger on Monday, saying it continues to believe the merger will damage writers and the industry, but as a nonprofit could not afford to proceed alone.

  • They allege they were persuaded not to exercise their contractual rights by former Vice executives who made fraudulent misrepresentations about the company's financial health and its failed sale to Antenna Group.

Paramount Must Release 30 Movies a Year to Close the Warner Deal
Twelve state attorneys general settled Monday, and Paramount also committed to spend $300 million more a year on U.S. film production than it did in 2025 and not to sell the Paramount or Warner lots.
Paramount settled the antitrust suit brought by 12 state attorneys general led by California's Rob Bonta, the last obstacle to its $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery. The consent decree (a court-enforced settlement) sets minimum annual film releases in the wide-release and tentpole categories and requires at least $300 million more a year on U.S. film production than Paramount spent in 2025. Remedies for breach include divestiture (a forced sale). A compliance monitor, an independent trustee and a five-state committee enforce it. Paramount rose 9 percent, Warner 10 percent.
Potential Talent Implication: A studio required by the settlement to release at least 30 films a year, and to spend more making them, has less room to shelve a finished picture or move a release date into the next fiscal year.
The Facts
  • Settlement reached Monday, Sept. 21, with 12 state AGs led by California's Rob Bonta. The WGA's separate suit is included in the settlement, per Deadline.
  • Movie commitments: minimum annual releases in the wide-release and "tentpole" categories; at least $300 million more annually on U.S. film production than 2025; commitments on pricing to theaters. Penalties for shortfall include potential divestiture. Deadline reports $1.5 billion total for home-grown film production, with additional domestic production required if a federal tax incentive passes. Reuters, cited by The Verge, reports a $30 million penalty per film against the 30-film annual pledge.
  • Lots: Paramount agreed to keep operations in California and not to sell the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots.
  • Labor: $47.5 million workforce development fund; obligation to honor existing collective bargaining agreements (Deadline).
  • Basic cable: separate distribution negotiations for Paramount and Warner Bros. basic cable channels for five years; restrictions on affiliate-fee negotiation changes and on using one party's confidential information in the other's negotiations; divestiture as a remedy for breach.
  • News: a News Editorial Independence Board for CNN and CBS News; an internal Compliance Monitor and an independent Monitoring Trustee; a five-state committee overseeing enforcement; the court retains jurisdiction.
  • Deal terms: $81 billion equity value, $110 billion enterprise value, $31 a share for WBD holders; $47 billion equity and $54 billion debt, with Larry Ellison personally guaranteeing the bulk of the equity. A $7 million-a-day ticking fee would have started Oct. 1.
  • Market: Paramount +9 percent; WBD +10 percent, about $30.50. $6 billion in promised cost savings; layoffs expected.

  • Opposition: the Block The Merger coalition called the settlement a capitulation; Mark Ruffalo said Gavin Newsom handed "a huge win to Trump."

A federal film and television tax incentive bill could be introduced as soon as next week, three sources told The Ankler, less than three weeks after President Trump endorsed the idea in an Aug. 31 Truth Social post. Representatives Laura Friedman and Linda Sanchez, California Democrats, are the likely co-leads with Republicans Brian Jack of Georgia and Nathaniel Moran of Texas. A Motion Picture Association study presented this week put U.S. production at 39 percent of global production and projected 65 percent under a federal credit.
Potential Talent Implication: More American production would mean more domestic work for the crews and casts who cannot follow a shoot to London, and a producer who can point to a federal credit has one fewer reason to argue a budget down.
The Facts
  • Three sources familiar with the matter say a bill could be introduced as soon as next week; some expect passage by year's end. Contours still unclear; Variety previously reported a 20 percent incentive.
  • Likely co-leads: Reps. Laura Friedman (D-CA), Linda Sanchez (D-CA), Brian Jack (R-GA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX). Friedman's district covers Glendale and Burbank; Jack's covers Trilith Studios.
  • MPA study, presented at a Capitol Hill press conference this week: a federal incentive could raise American production from 39 percent to 65 percent of global production and create more than 143,500 full-time jobs annually. Microsoft's Own Documents Call AI Training a Theft of Labor

Court documents unsealed Thursday in the suit brought by The New York Times and eleven other publishers against Microsoft and OpenAI show executives weighing whether their systems were built on stolen content. Microsoft director of applied science Brent Hecht called the ingestion of copyrighted works potentially "the largest theft of labor in human history." Nick Turley, OpenAI's head of ChatGPT, said "our products are largely substitutive, period." Internal Microsoft data shows the Times losing 87 to 93 percent of clicks through Bing Chat. The Facts
  • Documents unsealed Thursday, Sept. 17, in the litigation by The New York Times and eleven other publishers against Microsoft and OpenAI.
  • 2023 internal Microsoft document: "Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models 'hoovering up' all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions," noting that "almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use."
  • Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht described the ingestion of copyrighted works as "an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions" and potentially "the largest theft of labor in human history." Hecht also said a win on the copyright defense would "make a complete mockery of the idea of fair use."
  • An OpenAI engineer told president Greg Brockman of a "hack to get around [the] nytimes paywall" as the company explored scraping the site. Brockman: "Ah nice." Publishers argue employees were instructed to devise strategies to circumvent paywalls "without detection."
  • Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that "anything that is paywalled should be licensed by anyone who wants to use it," and said that had he known OpenAI scraped restricted content he would have "invoked" Microsoft's right to require retraining of the models.
  • Fair use is a four-factor test; OpenAI and Microsoft bear the burden. Supreme Court precedent holds that an "evasive motive" and violations of industry ethical standards undercut a fair use defense.
  • Fourth factor, market effect: Bing Chat copied all but two of the first 396 words of the Times's 2023 article "The Secrets Hamas knew about Israel's Military." An exhibit shows 100 other instances of GPT memorizing Times articles with word-for-word copying.
  • Internal Microsoft data: Times click-through rates fell 87 to 93 percent when users searched through Bing Chat rather than traditional web search.
  • Publishers argue Microsoft and OpenAI cannot claim no licensing market exists when they have signed deals with other publishers.

Private Equity Is Buying Literary Estates the Way It Bought Song Catalogs
International Literary Properties, funded by Viking Global, borrowed $100 million from Fifth Third Bank in January; Atticus Works launched this summer with $100 million from Primary Wave. Estates are fetching eight to 12 times annual royalties.
Two investment-backed buyers are assembling literary estates as an asset class. International Literary Properties, fully funded by Connecticut firm Viking Global, holds Tennessee Williams, Paddy Chayefsky, Langston Hughes, Evelyn Waugh and Ellen Raskin, and borrowed $100 million from Fifth Third Bank in January. Atticus Works launched this summer with $100 million from Primary Wave. Estates are selling at eight to 12 times annual royalties, against about 17 times for music catalogs, per Citrin Cooperman. ILP has Tennessee Williams productions set for New York and London and a Westing Game feature in development with a major studio.
Potential Talent Implication: Funds with return targets now sit on the seller's side of a backlist option, and they price the option and its renewal the way a catalog buyer prices a song.
The Facts
  • International Literary Properties launched in 2019, is now fully funded by Viking Global, and holds or manages estates including Tennessee Williams, Paddy Chayefsky, Langston Hughes, Evelyn Waugh, Ngaio Marsh, James Cain, Eric Ambler, Ed Emberley and Ellen Raskin. In Hughes and Chayefsky it owns a significant stake and manages.
  • ILP borrowed $100 million from Fifth Third Bank in January. CEO Michael Barra: "You know an asset class is maturing when a bank will offer you bank debt."
  • Atticus Works, founded this summer by investor and author Richard Hurowitz, launched with $100 million from Primary Wave, the private-equity-backed music publisher behind early catalog deals for Hall & Oates, Smokey Robinson, Kurt Cobain and Def Leppard. No acquisitions announced yet.
  • Precedent corporate deals: Netflix bought the Roald Dahl estate in 2021 for a reported $700 million; Embracer paid nearly $400 million for a piece of J.R.R. Tolkien rights.
  • Multiples: literary estates fetching eight to 12 times annual royalties; music catalogs peaked near 30 times for artists like Bruce Springsteen in the early 2020s and have settled around 17, per Citrin Cooperman. Jeffrey Archer, 86, has declined repeated offers at eight to 12 times, per his son James: "Guess we value them higher than the market."
  • Tax logic for sellers: converts royalty income taxed as ordinary income into a capital gain, and turns an illiquid asset into something an estate can divide.
  • Targets: deep backlists already generating revenue, from dead writers' estates, living writers near the end of a career, or mid-career authors simplifying. New books are out of scope. Buyers want 100 percent or close to it. About two-thirds of Big Five book sales are backlist, per Publishers Weekly.
  • Primary Wave CEO Larry Mestel: "We're only interested in one particular area of the business, which is the icon and legend business... Either the songs have to be iconic or the artists have to be legendary for us to buy the assets."
  • Short stories are treated as inventory rather than ballast; Prime Video greenlit a Stephen King short-story limited series this summer and Netflix did the same for a Roald Dahl adult collection. Manager Scott Glassgold has sold unpublished short stories for high six- and low seven-figure options.
  • Non-monetary deal points cited: estates excluding industries such as gambling or tobacco; one 50-title estate held back a single book from screen development.
  • Counter-view from agents and managers: the number of meaningful estates is finite, most have been "picked over through the years," and revenue growth is harder than a pitch deck suggests.

A24 Claimed Worldwide Rights to a Property Anyone Is Free to Copy
The SCP Foundation Wiki says A24 and Spooky Pictures never contacted it, and that the CC BY-SA 3.0 license bars exclusivity, DRM and any exclusive streaming window.
A24 and Spooky Pictures announced V/H/S: SCP, set in the SCP Foundation universe, with Deadline reporting A24 held worldwide rights. The SCP Foundation Wiki, which hosts the source material, says it was never contacted and that the material carries a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 license, which permits commercial derivative works only if the derivative carries the same license. Under those terms the film could not ship with DRM (copy protection), could not be distributed exclusively, and could be streamed by any service without payment. The Wiki says that is why no Hollywood film has used SCP material before.
Potential Talent Implication: The license on the underlying material sets what a buyer can actually sell, and on open-licensed source there is no exclusivity to grant, no window to hold and no streaming fee to share.
The Facts
  • Project: V/H/S: SCP, a new installment of the V/H/S horror anthology set in the SCP Foundation universe, announced with A24 attached and Spooky Pictures producing. Deadline reported A24 holding "worldwide rights."
  • License: the SCP Foundation, all SCPs and related concepts are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0. It permits commercial derivative works subject to the ShareAlike obligation: the derivative must itself be released under CC BY-SA 3.0 or later.
  • The Wiki's stated consequences if the film is a derivative work: no DRM or technological measures preventing copying; no distribution exclusivity, so any commercial streaming service could stream it without payment to anyone and anyone could upload it to YouTube; no ability to stop other parties making their own SCP works or derivatives of this film; no terms on theaters preventing them from making copies. Violating the license forfeits all rights to distribute any SCP-derived work.
  • Contact: "we have not had any communication with the filmmakers, producers, or distributors for this project, despite our best efforts, and to the best of our knowledge they have not made any efforts to contact us." Wiki admin DrEverettMann told The Verge: "We have made several attempts to contact them since the announcement of the project but haven't received a response."
  • The Wiki's stated ask: either release the film under CC BY-SA 3.0 or later and take no hostile action against license-compliant parties, or release it with no SCP-derived content. It states no preference between the two and says it is not seeking money: "We do not have the legal ability to do so, and would not even if we could."
  • Derivative-work scope: the Wiki says a film using no existing SCP anomalies would still be a derivative work, comparing it to new Star Trek series with new casts and ships.
  • Precedent: the Wiki states this license structure "is why, despite prior interest, no Hollywood films have been created using SCP material."
  • Statement page last edited September 15, 2026. SCP International, the common organization for all SCP language branches, issued a joint statement.
  • A24's Backrooms, also originating on 4chan, was made with the creator of a YouTube series popular in that community, per The Verge.

The UK Writers Guild President Wants Undeclared AI in a Script Treated as Fraud
Jack Thorne told the Writers' Guild of Great Britain that a studio should be able to sue a writer who delivers an AI-generated script without declaring it, and asked the BBC and Channel 4 to add their own sanctions.
Jack Thorne, who wrote Adolescence and serves as WGGB president, said in a speech titled Authorship in the Age of AI that executives and writers close to him describe writers using AI "to cheat." He drew the line at replacement rather than assistance: discussion, spellcheck and layout are fine, prompts in place of writing are not. "Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful," he said, and a studio that commissioned the script "should have the right to take me to court."
Potential Talent Implication: Thorne is asking for a rule that turns the authorship warranty in a writing agreement from boilerplate into a term a studio could sue on, and the line he draws between assistance and replacement is where that warranty would sit.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Jack Thorne, WGGB president, writer of Adolescence, Lord of the Flies and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. Speech titled Authorship in the Age of AI.
  • Thorne: "I have spoken to a number of execs and studio heads about their use of AI, and got hugely different responses, but what I did hear from them, and what anecdotally I've heard from a few writers close to me, is that some in my profession are using AI to cheat."
  • The distinction he draws: "What I'm not talking about here is using AI to help: To discuss things with, to check for spelling errors or help with layout. I'm talking about using AI as a replacement for endeavour, as a replacement for writing at all."
  • His proposed legal standard: "Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful. If you use AI to generate content and you do not declare it as such, then that is fraud and the companies you do it to should be entitled to prosecute you."
  • His worked example: "If I excitedly pitch my Mars show to Netflix and they send me to script, and I write the script using AI and do not tell them, then they should have the right to take me to court."
  • Industry sanction: he called on the BBC and Channel 4 to act on discoveries, comparing the consequence to university expulsion for AI-written essays.
  • On training data: big tech should publish its data sets with "audited summaries of every input that has led to their outputs." Thorne: "Big tech steal, but because they don't have to declare where they stole from, the stealing goes unpunished."
  • Government response: a spokesperson said copyright laws "must protect the UK's position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation."

CBS Says Dropping a Writer Is Protected Creative Speech
John Lowe's Matlock deal guaranteed 20 weeks and then ran week to week at the studio's discretion, and CBS says the decision not to extend it shaped the scripts.
CBS Television Studios moved Friday to dismiss claims in writer John Lowe's suit under California's anti-SLAPP law, which allows early dismissal of claims that chill free speech. Lowe alleges a hostile work environment and retaliatory firing after he reported that a supervisor called Juneteenth "Coonteenth." CBS lawyer Adam Levin wrote that staffing judgments "are creative, because the composition of the room determines the content of the scripts that are shot for exhibition to the public." CBS says Lowe was never terminated: his deal guaranteed 20 weeks, then continued week to week.
Potential Talent Implication: The guaranteed-weeks term is the part of a staff writing deal a studio cannot recast as a creative judgment, and everything past it runs at the studio's discretion.
The Facts
  • CBS Television Studios filed the motion on Friday, September 11, under California's anti-SLAPP statute, seeking early dismissal of some claims.
  • Lowe alleges Matlock's showrunner and executive producers created a workplace "permeated by sexually explicit and discriminatory conduct," and that he was terminated after reporting the Juneteenth remark.
  • CBS argument, per outside counsel Adam Levin: "A writer who is performing well and having a positive impact on the scripts may be extended, while a writer who is not performing well is generally let go earlier. Those judgments are creative, because the composition of the room determines the content of the scripts that are shot for exhibition to the public."
  • Contract structure per the motion: 20 guaranteed weeks, then week to week at CBS's discretion. CBS says it declined to extend rather than terminated.
  • CBS detailed alleged performance issues: failure to follow writing assignments, outlines that did not incorporate notes or capture the show's tone, late arrivals to set and departures during shooting, all documented with human resources.
  • Executive producer Nicki Renna said in a declaration that flashbacks in a Lowe outline "did not work" and "another scene did not make sense."
  • Showrunner Jennie Snyder Urman said in a declaration that the "Coonteenth" claim was "made up" by Lowe.
  • CBS Studios statement: "confident that Lowe's accusations are demonstrably inaccurate and maliciously fabricated" and "we stand firmly behind our producers."

Row K paid a reported eight figures for Cliffhanger at Toronto last year and then imploded; Vertical has taken US rights and is targeting a wide spring 2027 release.
Vertical acquired US rights to Jaume Collet-Serra's Cliffhanger reboot, starring Pierce Brosnan and Lily James, and is targeting a wide spring 2027 theatrical release. Row K, the buzzy new distributor at last year's Toronto festival, bought the film for a reported eight figures and then collapsed, leaving Cliffhanger and other titles it had acquired without a home. The expectation around Cannes was that Neon's new Decal label would take it. Vertical partner Peter Jarowey negotiated with SVP of Acquisitions Tony Piantedosi and Manager of Acquisitions Rachel White; CAA Media Finance represented the filmmakers.

Studios Stopped Developing and the Ideas Moved Outside
CAA's Roeg Sutherland told TIFF's new market that studios have stopped developing the way they used to and that the ideas directors and actors want are not coming through traditional routes.
At TIFF: The Market, CAA Co-Head of Media Finance Roeg Sutherland said studio development has contracted and that talent is hunting material outside the usual pipeline: "All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes." He said the market now resets every two weeks rather than every six months. FilmNation CEO Glen Basner said independent distributors package to reduce risk by pre-selling to streamers, which builds films for streaming rather than a theatrical proposition.
Potential Talent Implication: When studios stop developing, the person holding the underlying material sets the terms of the package, and the option and the attachment now carry the leverage the development deal used to.
The Facts
  • Panel at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto International Film Festival's new film and TV market, with TIFF's Geoff Macnaughton.
  • Roeg Sutherland, Co-Head of Media Finance, CAA: "It's cyclical, [but] what is happening now is that things are changing so much quicker than they ever have. Instead of having to reset yourself every six months, you have to reset yourself every two weeks."
  • Sutherland: "Things will be uncomfortable, but we work in independent film; everything's uncomfortable pretty much all the time."
  • Sutherland: "Studios are not developing the way they used to, which presents an unbelievable opportunity to the independent community. All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes."
  • Glen Basner, CEO, FilmNation Entertainment, on independent distributors: "This is my biggest complaint about the independent distribution community right now. There's a very traditional approach to packaging. They're worried about how much risk they're taking, and so they know they need to mitigate that by selling their movie to pay television, and specifically to streamers. The only problem is that we're [then] building movies for the streamer companies. That may work great on streaming, but it's not the same thing as building a theatrical proposition."
  • Basner: "We are trying to evolve to say, 'how do we make the best possible film so that it can compel people, in an undeniable way, to see it in a movie theater?' And if they do go and see it, then it's going to work in home video, it's going to work on pay TV, it's going to work on free television."
  • Basner on theatrical: "I think 2027 is going to be a great year at the theatrical box office."

Creators Are Selling Tools Around the Archive, Not Just the Newsletter

Puck reports that former Substack executives Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine have launched a consultancy, Spur, arguing that creator businesses need products beyond newsletters, podcasts and events as AI aggregation erodes search and social traffic. Tedesco said AI now makes personalized tools cheap enough for creators to build against their own archives. The Facts
  • Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine, two former Substack executives, are launching a consultancy called Spur. The news was broken by Emily Sundberg's Feed Me.

  • Tedesco: "This is not A.I. slop. This is not A.I. writing. This is a further progression of technology making creativity better and more accessible. This is a thing I wasn't able to build a year ago, and it's a thing that Sean wouldn't be able to, or maybe even want to, build himself." (Referring to a hypothetical bot serving The Ringer's Sean Fennessey's movie recommendations.)
  • Tedesco: "Let us build the tools to think about growth for you in what we think will be the highest-leverage way, not just the way that is generally recommended."

YouTube Is Showing NFL Games Without Buying NFL Rights
YouTube ingested Peacock Premium into YouTube Premium in late July, delivering a full NFL season including postseason, plus NBA, MLB and the Olympics, without licensing a single game from the league.
Under a late-July agreement, YouTube pays Comcast an undisclosed wholesale fee per subscriber per month to carry Peacock Premium inside YouTube Premium, putting NFL games in front of tens of millions of YouTube subscribers with no rights deal and no production cost.   • Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch on last month's earnings call: "we will not be making any amendments to our existing [NFL] contractual relationship... We don't see any changes to our contractual terms until the 2030 season."

Warner Bros Motion Picture chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy sat with TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey on Friday and described their model as building repeat business with filmmakers. The Facts

  • Closing estimate unchanged at the first half of 2027.
  • Nallen on the combination: Roku is at an "inflection point," starting to accelerate growth; Tubi has recently turned profitable while revenue keeps surging. "It's going to end up as a superb transaction."
  • Leverage ratio expected at 2.8 times trailing earnings, with rapid deleveraging. Share buyback of $1 billion to $1.5 billion to proceed "unabated."

Florida Says Netflix Sold an Ad-Free Promise and Built an Ad Business
Florida's attorney general sued Netflix in state court Wednesday, alleging it collected roughly 550 billion events a day as early as 2016 and later monetized that data through the ad tier it launched in 2022.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed suit under state unfair and deceptive practices law, seeking damages and an order forcing Netflix to stop collecting and monetizing user data. The complaint says Netflix marketed itself as kid-friendly and ad-free, citing a 2019 shareholder letter calling the absence of ads "a deep part of our brand proposition," while logging some 550 billion events per day as early as 2016. It alleges autoplay was designed to extend viewing, and that advertisers can match their own data to Netflix profiles carrying education, marital status and household income. Netflix says it complies with privacy law.
Potential Talent Implication: Netflix's engagement data is the basis for every renewal and bonus decision a producer cannot audit, and a state action seeking to bar its collection puts a court, rather than a negotiation, on the question of what that data is and who it belongs to.
The Facts
  • Filed Wednesday in Florida state court by Attorney General James Uthmeier, alleging violations of state law on unfair and deceptive practices. Seeks unspecified damages, an order to cease collecting and monetizing user data, and interface changes.
  • Complaint: "Netflix's years-long bait-and-switch has led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts."
  • Data scale alleged: roughly 550 billion events per day as early as 2016, covering searches, pauses, rewatches, browsing and scrolling behavior and device information.
  • Quoted in the complaint, a Netflix engineer in 2016: "We're really a [data] logging company ... a logging company that occasionally streams movies."
  • The 2019 shareholder letter cited describes the absence of ads as "a deep part of our brand proposition." Netflix launched its ad business in 2022.
  • Advertising claims: advertisers can connect their own data with Netflix profiles for targeting; the operation includes demographic and lifestyle information such as education, marital status, and household income and makeup.
  • Design claims: autoplay deliberately designed to extend viewing; obstructed cancellations; deterrence of privacy-protective settings; behavioral advertising representations regarding kids profiles.
  • Uthmeier: "Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false."
  • Netflix response: the company takes "members' privacy seriously" and complies with privacy and data-protection laws everywhere we operate.
  • Context: Uthmeier has also sued TikTok and OpenAI this year and opted out of a $17 billion multi-state settlement with Meta.

Warner Bros. Discovery Tripled What It Spends Guarding Its CEO
Warner Bros. Discovery's executive security spending rose more than 200% to $3.2 million last year. Disney and Netflix each spent $1.8 million, up more than 30%; Amazon spent $1.7 million, up more than 50%.

  • The Security Executive Council: by October 31, 2025, documented physical and cyberattacks targeting senior corporate executives had already doubled the previous year's total.
  • Incident cited: at 3:45 a.m. on April 10, a man threw an incendiary device over the fence at OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's home. It bounced off the house; no one was hurt. Altman posted about it the same morning.

Channel 4 will merge documentaries and factual entertainment, reality and entertainment, and specialist factual into one unit, putting about half of commissioning roles at risk within the 340-job cut announced Wednesday.

Toronto's New Market Moves Indie Financing Three Months Earlier
The TIFF market runs September 10 to 16 with more than 150 exhibitors, and sellers told Deadline they will assemble finance plans this fall and start cameras in January.
Toronto launched a formal market alongside the festival this year, running through September 16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre with an advisory committee that includes CAA Media Finance co-head Roeg Sutherland, Mubi SVP of global distribution Arianna Bocco and Sony Pictures Classics co-president Michael Barker. One indie label boss told Deadline that presale contracts struck at November's American Film Market arrive too late to take to a bank until the following year, while Toronto lets a financing plan come together over the fall and production start in January. Deadline reports AFM would become the place those contracts close.
Potential Talent Implication: Financing that closes in the fall puts cameras up in January, which moves the start date and the availability window in a director or cast deal six months ahead of where the AFM calendar used to put them.
The Facts
  • The TIFF market runs September 10 to 16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre with some 150-plus exhibitors.
  • Advisory committee members named by Deadline: CAA Media Finance co-head Roeg Sutherland, Mubi SVP global distribution Arianna Bocco, Sony Pictures Classics co-founder and co-president Michael Barker.
  • One indie label boss: "One of the frustrations out of [November's American Film Market] is that by the time you did presales to finance a project, those contracts aren't signed and I can't actually go to bank. I can't do anything until later next year. Whereas in Toronto, you can spend your fall putting your finance plan together and boom go into production at the start of January."
  • One seller: "We were already treating Toronto like a market."
  • Last year's Toronto acquisition Obsession reached $512 million worldwide, the highest-grossing festival acquisition on record. Deadline reports the result is "largely felt to be an anomaly."
  • A24's Sundance pickup The Invite grossed more than $55 million worldwide.
  • Black Bear took Sydney Sweeney boxing title Christy off the sales market and self-distributed it; it grossed less than $2 million domestically after an early-November release. Searchlight's The Testament of Ann Lee took $2.5 million domestic.

  • In 2022 CAA Media Finance and Miramax orchestrated a $30 million global sale for Alexander Payne's The Holdovers, which drew five Oscar nominations.
  • TIFF cut Press and Industry screenings from two per title to one because the market took showtimes.
  • Apple's Being Heumann opened the festival; Amazon MGM's I Play Rocky plays Saturday night.

A Documentary That Names Its Abusers Is Harder to Sue
California's Second District Court of Appeal reversed the trial court on Thursday and dismissed Dan Schneider's defamation suit against Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television over Quiet on Set.
The panel found the docuseries "clearly distinguishes" between the gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior and sexual innuendo its participants attribute to Schneider and the child sexual abuse it attributes to three named individuals, and noted the series told viewers a Nickelodeon investigation found no evidence of abuse by him. A Los Angeles Superior Court judge had let the case proceed in 2024 after finding viewers could draw "damning implications." Schneider had sought damages and an order removing portions of the series or taking it down entirely. Gibson Dunn handled the appeal for Warner Bros.
Potential Talent Implication: A documentary that says plainly who did what is protected even where the editing invites a darker reading, which is what a filmmaker's insurer and its on-camera participants are relying on when they agree to name a living subject.
The Facts
  • California's Second District Court of Appeal ruled Thursday, September 10, reversing a 2024 decision by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Ashfaq G. Chowdhury that had allowed the suit to proceed.
  • From the decision: "The documentary clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider, gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior, and inappropriate sexual innuendo, and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals."
  • The court said it would "refrain from splitting hairs to find an allegation of child sexual abuse where the only such abuse discussed is explicitly attributed to named perpetrators and the documentary expressly states that an investigation into Schneider found no evidence of abuse."
  • Schneider had targeted the editing: episode two introduces abusers Brian Peck and Jason Handy while cutting to images of Schneider. The panel reviewed the segment and found roughly six minutes focused on Handy with no time given to Schneider in those scenes.
  • "Schneider's attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing," the order stated.
  • Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV debuted in 2024 on Max and Investigation Discovery. In episode three, Drake Bell came forward as the anonymous victim in the case against dialogue coach Brian Peck, convicted in 2004.
  • Defendants named in the complaint: Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television.
  • Warners' appeal was handled by Theodore J. Boutrous, Ilissa Samplin, Zachary C. Freund and Connor S. Sullivan of Gibson Dunn. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and the International Documentary Association filed amicus briefs supporting the studio.
  • Schneider lawyer Gerry Silver said the producer is evaluating "options for further review and appeal."

Texas Has $1.5 Billion in Film Rebates and a Company Selling Help Claiming It
Goldenrod went live Thursday for Texas productions with pilots in Kentucky and Louisiana, charging a deposit plus a percentage of the incentive money it captures for film, television, commercial and game shoots.
The Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program passed last fall set a $1.5 billion fund paying $300 million every two years for a decade. The base rate runs 5% to 25% depending on in-state spend above a $250,000 minimum, with uplifts available, and it pays as a cash rebate, which lands faster than a tax credit. At least 60% of production must happen in state and 35% of cast and crew must be Texas residents. Co-founder Russell Wayne Groves said about 10 productions beta tested the service, whose founders include a former Texas Film Commission incentives lead.
Potential Talent Implication: A residency floor and an in-state spend floor decide whether a rebate pays at all, so the hiring plan and the shooting schedule are where a producer's incentive money is won or lost before a single term is negotiated.
The Facts
  • Goldenrod launched Thursday, September 10, live for Texas productions with pilot projects in Kentucky and Louisiana. It covers film, television, commercial and video game productions.
  • Business model: a deposit upfront plus a percentage of incentives captured.
  • The expanded Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program, passed last fall, established a $1.5 billion fund, or $300 million every two years for a decade.
  • Base incentive rate is 5% to 25% depending on in-state spend, with a $250,000 minimum and uplifts possible. It is a cash rebate system, which pays out faster than a tax incentive.
  • At least 60% of production must be completed in state. Texas has a 35% residency requirement for cast and crew.
  • Co-founder Russell Wayne Groves, founder of The Ranch Productions in Austin: "Incentives compliance is genuinely hard to get right. The administrative load pulls you off set, off the creative work, and if you miss something, you're either leaving significant dollars on the table or facing disqualification entirely." He compared the service to "a TurboTax for production incentives."
  • Groves on the residency math: "So, if you were at 30% and you were on week four of five, you'd... need to hire an extra five people to fit in that box. That is what we're trying to flag."
  • Other founders: Ted Griffis and Brandon Thomas of Austin post house TBD Post, and Tara Khanna, former Incentives Team Lead and Senior Production Incentives Specialist at the Texas Film Commission.
  • Groves onboarded his own SXSW-premiering film Stages first; about 10 productions beta tested.

Ten States Have Pulled Back the Tax Breaks They Gave Data Centers
New Jersey cancelled $250 million in AI and data center credits in August, Illinois suspended its program for two years from July 1, and the governors of Ohio and Texas moved against their own exemptions.
Newsweek counted action across ten states. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker suspended new data center incentives for two years beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications in May. Texas Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions in June, arguing developers should cover more power and infrastructure costs. Virginia kept its exemption but added a tax of $0.011 per kilowatt hour on data center electricity. Minnesota repealed its electricity exemption effective July 2025. Arizona, Georgia and Michigan have bills pending; Washington narrowed its exemptions through Senate Bill 6231.
Potential Talent Implication: State legislatures that spent a decade defending tech subsidies are now repealing them, which is the same political test a film and television incentive has to pass every session it comes up for renewal.
The Facts
  • Newsweek, published September 9, 2026, documents action in Arizona, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Washington.
  • New Jersey enacted the "End Data Center Tax Credits Act" in August 2026, eliminating the remaining $250 million available for AI and data center projects under the Next New Jersey Program.
  • Illinois: Governor JB Pritzker announced a two-year suspension of new data center incentives beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs.
  • Ohio: Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications for the sales tax exemption in May 2026.
  • Texas: Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions and other data center incentives in June 2026. No repeal has been enacted.
  • Virginia: Senator Danica Roem's proposed repeal (S.B. 30) projected roughly $1 billion in additional general fund revenue in year one and $1.1 billion in year two. It was not enacted; the 2026 budget compromise kept the exemption and added a $0.011 per kilowatt hour tax on data center electricity consumption.
  • Minnesota repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity used by qualified data centers, effective for purchases after June 30, 2025.
  • Washington's Senate Bill 6231 removed exemptions for replacement server equipment and ended eligibility for certain refurbished data centers, keeping incentives for qualifying new facilities.
  • Arizona Senate Bills 1463 and 1467 and House Bill 2820 would repeal the state's data center certification program. Georgia Senate Bill 410 would stop new exemption certificates. Michigan House Bills 5396 and 5398 target the sales tax exemption and property tax treatment. None has been enacted.
  • Newsweek reports the stated objections are electricity demand, water consumption, grid infrastructure costs and lost tax revenue, and that incentive programs have cost more than originally projected as AI demand grew. Newsweek says it contacted the Data Center Coalition for comment and was awaiting a response.

McClatchy Cut More Than 90 Journalists Months After Pushing Them Onto AI
Unions estimated more than 90 journalists lost jobs Thursday across at least 13 papers in eight states, including over 30 positions at the Miami Herald and a third of unionized staff in the Pacific Northwest.
An internal memo, first shared publicly by the New York Times' Katie Robertson, said consumer revenue fell 41% while local news expenses stayed flat, and that "the status quo no longer works." Earlier this year more than 30 Sacramento Bee staffers said they would withhold bylines from work produced by McClatchy's "content scaling agent," a generative tool that let editors republish reporters' existing work under new headlines. NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss said the 41% figure "needs to be verified." McClatchy did not respond to TheWrap and had made no public announcement as of Thursday afternoon.
Potential Talent Implication: A tool that republishes a writer's existing work under new headlines is a use of that work, and the byline strike at the Sacramento Bee shows the credit is the only place a staff writer can price it.
The Facts
  • Layoffs hit McClatchy newsrooms nationwide on Thursday, September 10. Unions estimated more than 90 journalists affected across at least 13 papers in eight states.
  • Carol Marbin Miller, deputy investigations editor at the Miami Herald, said McClatchy "wrote off more than 30 positions" there, "well over one-third of its editorial staff," including several accountability beats.
  • The Pacific Northwest Newspaper Guild said it was "shocked and disappointed" by cuts to 33% of unionized workers at the Idaho Statesman, The News Tribune (Tacoma), Tri-City Herald, The Olympian and Bellingham Herald, including 10 journalists in Idaho and seven in Washington.
  • The Charlotte Observer reported eight employees laid off, about a quarter of its newsroom.
  • Internal memo, first shared publicly by New York Times reporter Katie Robertson: an internal analysis found consumer revenue declined 41% while local news expenses remained flat. "We are making these changes because the status quo no longer works. We cannot continue investing where subscriber interest does not support the investment."
  • Earlier in 2026, more than 30 Sacramento Bee staffers said they would withhold their bylines from stories created by McClatchy's "content scaling agent," a generative AI product that produces new pieces using reporters' existing work.
  • Ariane Lange, investigative reporter and vice chair of the Bee's union, said management promoted the tool as a way to boost traffic and productivity, and that it allowed editors to produce repurposed versions of previous work under new headlines.
  • NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss said the 41% decline "needs to be verified," and wrote: "McClatchy execs decided to push AI slop on news sites. You can't pivot to AI, cut 40% of your local journalists and write 'we remain deeply committed to local journalism.' You're lying."
  • New York Times media reporter Ben Mullin: "This is one of the bleakest media layoff memos I've seen in 12 years covering the industry."
  • McClatchy is 168 years old and owns the Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald and the Charlotte Observer among others. Representatives did not respond to TheWrap.

The Federal Film Credit Has Bill Language and No Time to Pass It
The working figure is a 20 percent credit that could rise another 5 to 10 points for rural filming or for spreading spend across states, and Congress leaves for the midterms within days.
Senator Adam Schiff's office told Deadline that bill language exists for a federal film and TV incentive and that Senate, House and Trump administration leaders are finalizing text. The working number is a 20 percent credit, rising at least 5 to 10 points for rural filming or spend spread across several states. Drafters modeled it on California's $750 million annual program, and some language comes from suggestions David Ellison put to members of Congress privately. Both chambers recess for the midterms in days, and the measure must clear the Joint Committee on Taxation.

The Facts
  • Schiff spokesperson: "There is bill language, and currently, leaders in the Senate, House, and Trump administration are engaging in conversations to finalize text." And: "Negotiations are ongoing."
  • Working figure: 20 percent credit, plus at least 5 to 10 points for rural-area filming or spreading production spend across several states.
  • Bill name: the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a Trump-coined title.
  • House sponsors: Linda Sanchez (D-CA, Ways and Means) and Laura Friedman (D-CA, ex-Rysher Entertainment, Schiff's successor in Burbank). Republicans Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Brian Jack (R-GA) are also in the mix.
  • Structure modeled on California's $750 million annual program, including a menu of redemption methods over several years. Relocation provision targets series or films first made outside the country, or content already assured foreign credits that has not started production.

Paramount Paid Over $100 Million for a Movie It Has Not Dated
Trey Parker and Matt Stone's untitled musical, known inside Paramount as Whitney Springs, was picked up in January 2022 as a negative pickup, lost two release dates and came off the schedule entirely last November.
Paramount committed more than $100 million to an untitled Trey Parker and Matt Stone feature through a negative pickup, a deal where the studio buys a finished film and the filmmakers keep whatever is left of the budget, Matthew Frank reported in The Ankler. One person familiar put the total at $150 million; another put it between $70 and $80 million. Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free produce and Lamar wrote original, unreleased songs. Paramount dated the picture for July 4, 2025, moved it to March 20, 2026, then took it off the schedule last November.
Potential Talent Implication: A negative pickup pays the filmmakers at delivery and lets them keep what they did not spend, so Parker and Stone have their nine-figure money while the picture sits undated and every part of a deal that pays on release stays unpaid.
The Facts
  • Project: untitled feature written by South Park veteran Vernon Chatman, directed by Trey Parker, produced by Matt Stone, Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free. Known internally at Paramount as Whitney Springs. Parker plays the town's mayor.
  • Premise: a musical comedy about reparations for slavery, set at a historical slave plantation museum in the Midwest, following a young Black re-enactor who clashes with the town's racist mayor.
  • Deal: "Paramount committed more than $100 million to the project through a negative pickup - where the creators keep what is left from the budget." One source put the total cost at $150 million; another put the deal terms between $70 and $80 million.
  • The budget was defrayed across multiple Paramount divisions, including Chris McCarthy's cable group. The film has no A-list cast or heavy visual effects; "whatever the filmmakers didn't spend, they kept."
  • Timeline: Paramount execs read the script at Park County in late 2021; the studio picked it up in January 2022. Then-Paramount Pictures head Brian Robbins called it "one of the funniest and most original scripts we've ever read" at CinemaCon 2024. Set for July 4, 2025; moved in March 2025 to March 20, 2026; removed from the schedule in November 2025; unmentioned at David Ellison's first CinemaCon in April 2026.
  • Statement from Stone and Parker: "We take full responsibility for the schedule delay of this movie. We apologize to our partners at pgLang and Paramount and we appreciate their patience. South Park and life's circumstances have gotten in the way but we still believe in the project."
  • Paramount declined to comment; pgLang did not respond.
  • People close to the production called Lamar's music among the strongest elements and described early cuts as "really rough." No source said Ellison ordered a delay over the film's politics.
  • Context: Parker and Stone's five-year, $500-$550 million HBO Max streaming deal expired in 2025; after a public fight they signed a five-year, $1.5 billion contract for South Park streaming rights plus 10 new episodes a year in July 2025.
  • Comparable undated comedies: Warner Bros.' Animal Friends with Ryan Reynolds, pushed four times, most recently to January 22, 2027; Jonah Hill's Cut Off, pulled from July 17 with no new date.
  • Paramount has 12 films dated for 2027 and seven for 2028.

Creators Wrote Their Own AI Definitions Before the Studios Did
The Standards & Definitions Project launched Wednesday with a glossary of about 180 AI terms and a visualizer scoring roughly 150 creative jobs from 0 to 5 on AI replacement.
The Creators Coalition on AI, founded nine months ago by Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Daniel Kwan and late-night veteran Ted Tremper, launched a public Standards & Definitions Project on Wednesday. It carries a glossary of roughly 180 AI terms and an AI Impact Visualizer rating about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, including directing, sound, animation, writing and acting, from 0 (does not touch the job) to 5 (could do the whole job). More than 250 people have been polled and most roles still read "required knowledge." Founders say the shared terms are meant for guild negotiations and individual talent deals.
Potential Talent Implication: Human-authored content and AI digital performance now have written definitions that did not come off a studio's paper, and those are the terms a deal about AI use will be argued in.
The Facts
  • Launch date: Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Project name: the Standards & Definitions Project, run by the Creators Coalition on AI (CCAI).
  • Glossary: approximately 180 AI terms.
  • AI Impact Visualizer: about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, scored 0 to 5 on likelihood of AI role replacement. Many roles broken into dozens of sub-categories.
  • More than 250 people polled to date; the project targets responses in the thousands. Major updates planned quarterly. A survey page vets users to confirm they work in Hollywood.
  • CCAI founded December 2025 by Gordon-Levitt, Kwan, Ted Tremper and more than a dozen others. Thousands of signatories including Judd Apatow, Ava DuVernay, Margot Robbie, Guillermo del Toro and Hiro Murai. David Goyer is a founder and the group's secretary.
  • Two conventions were held this summer with guild-based delegates from all 11 areas; the most recent concluded ten days before launch.
  • Sample definition, human-authored content: "Creative work in which no generative AI system contributed expressive content, irrespective of the technological tools otherwise used in its creation, capture, processing, or distribution."
  • Sample definition, AI Digital Performance: "the application of artificial intelligence to capture, synthesize, modify, and/or replicate a human being or animal performer's natural person's human individual's performance attributes, which can include visual and physiological likeness, both still and kinetic facial expression, body movement, biometric characteristics, choreography, and voice whether partially or in full."
  • Tremper: "The purpose of these resources is take all the things we hear about with regard to AI and establish ground truth." He also cited a use case in drafting statehouse bills.
  • Gordon-Levitt: "Artists and content creators are a canary in the coal mine."
  • Kwan: "If we're going to be fighting for transparency, we should also be modeling it."

Blizzard Workers Won the Right to Bargain Over AI at Work
Roughly 1,900 Blizzard workers ratified first contracts Tuesday night that require management to bargain over workplace AI, add four weeks of severance and give laid-off staff 14 months of recall rights.
Blizzard Entertainment workers on World of Warcraft, Hearthstone, Overwatch and Diablo ratified their first union contracts Tuesday night after two years of negotiations, according to the Communications Workers of America. The deals cover about 1,900 people and include wage increases, grievance procedures, just cause disciplinary protections, a three-day in-office week, four additional weeks of severance, and a right to be recalled to an open role within 14 months of a layoff announcement. They also require the company to bargain over the use of AI in the workplace. Microsoft, which owns Blizzard, cut 3,200 Xbox roles in July.
Potential Talent Implication: AI use became a bargaining subject rather than a management announcement, and a layoff acquired a price through 14 months of recall rights and four extra weeks of severance, at a company whose parent cut 3,200 games jobs two months earlier.
