Overall deals now average $2 million a year, and Seth MacFarlane asked NBCUniversal to downgrade his own
Netflix's new five-year Shonda Rhimes deal is one of the last in the nine-figure range. J.J. Abrams' $250 million Warner Bros. overall came back as a two-year first-look.
CEO Summary
The Ankler interviewed a dozen studio, streaming, business affairs, agency and showrunner sources on how overall deals have changed since Peak TV ended. Annual value capped at $4 million to $5 million a decade ago and now averages $2 million, with a $20 million to $50 million tier held by a named handful. Guaranteed money is being replaced by success bonuses. Sources say Seth MacFarlane asked NBCUniversal to convert his five-year, $200 million exclusive into a first-look so he could sell animation elsewhere.
Why This Matters
MacFarlane's move puts a price on exclusivity that did not previously exist as a stated term. He gave back guarantee and bought the right to sell animation to any buyer, a trade that pays only if his output has more than one plausible home.

Everything else in the reporting describes studios reducing their own risk. A lit agent traces the overall deal itself to Apple, Amazon and Netflix arriving in the legacy space and paying up front to take writers away from it. That premium has been withdrawn. What replaced it moves the downside onto the creator.
Specific Implication
Writers negotiating an overall should price the bonus architecture rather than the guarantee: what triggers a kicker, whether renewal and awards bonuses stack, and whether a kicker survives a cancellation decision.
The Facts
  • A decade ago overall deals capped at $4 million to $5 million a year, with top showrunners earning that upfront plus roughly $4 million in backend profit participation. Most deals now average $2 million annually. The $20 million to $50 million tier covers Mike Schur at NBCUniversal, Alex Kurtzman at Paramount, Shonda Rhimes at Netflix and Ryan Murphy at Disney.
  • Netflix announced a third Rhimes deal last week, a five-year exclusive with undisclosed terms that sources say is likely one of the few remaining nine-figure pacts. Rhimes left Disney in 2017 for a four-year, $100 million Netflix exclusive that produced Bridgerton.
  • A studio executive: "Every deal we've done since Peak TV ended is less money. There are few people getting raises in deals. It's a lesser guarantee but higher kickers (bonuses)."
  • MacFarlane signed a five-year, $200 million NBCUniversal deal in 2020. Sources say he asked to convert it to a first-look. His guaranteed upfront was cut sharply, the deal still covers Fuzzy Door salaries and overhead, and success bonuses could still reach a similar total. A studio source noted that if NBCU passes and Netflix buys, Netflix produces in-house rather than paying a licensing fee, which matters most in animation "where the licensing fees can skyrocket."
  • J.J. Abrams' Bad Robot signed a five-year, $250 million film and TV overall with Warner Bros. in 2019. On expiry in 2024 it was renewed as a two-year first-look expiring this year. "They weren't getting a return," a cable executive said.
  • Steve Levitan's $125 million, five-year deal at Disney's 20th Television quietly expired after Hulu's Reboot and a season of Netflix's Nobody Wants This. Ava DuVernay's Warner Bros. TV deal has also expired.
  • John Wells renewed at Warner Bros. TV with a sizable upfront plus bonuses tied to episode volume. Shawn Ryan signed a four-year, eight-figure Netflix deal in 2024 loaded with incentives. Courtney Kemp exited Netflix for Apple after delivering Nemesis.
  • Matt and Ross Duffer signed with Paramount last year, a film and TV deal sources estimate at nine figures over four years, with cost split between Paramount Television Studios and the film division. Liz Tigelaar signed a joint pact across Paramount TV and CBS Studios.
  • Eric Heisserer, co-showrunner on Peacock's Dungeon Crawler Carl, has signed a show-tied first-look with NBCU, reported exclusively by The Ankler. Haley Z. Boston is in talks for an overall with Netflix.
  • Emmy kickers run $25,000 to $100,000. One deal pays $50,000 for a series nomination, $25,000 for a writing nomination and $25,000 for a directing nomination.
  • One showrunner traded a "generational deal" in the high eight figures for a renewal in the high seven to low eight figures plus success bonuses.

The Justice Department told a federal court that training AI on copyrighted work is fair use
The government's lead argument is national security. The brief says AI analyzes intelligence and recommends missile targets, and that training limits would hand an advantage to foreign adversaries.
CEO Summary
The Justice Department filed a brief in New York federal court on Tuesday backing OpenAI against The New York Times, arguing that training on copyrighted material is fair use. The Hollywood Reporter reports this appears to be the government's first position on the question, in a set of cases that also involves music publishers, news publishers and studios. The brief separately argues that requiring licenses would entrench legacy media owners, because only the largest technology companies could afford the fees.
Why This Matters
The government's competition argument lands on rights holders. It treats a market for training licenses as a barrier that protects whoever owns the deepest catalog, which describes the studios and publishers now trying to sell exactly that license. The brief binds no court. It is still a citable federal position on the question that decides whether a training license is legally required or commercially optional, and anyone negotiating one should expect to hear it quoted back.
Specific Implication
An AI training license should carry consideration for access, data quality, metadata, indemnity and exclusivity, so the agreement holds value if a court later finds that permission was never required.
The Facts
  • The brief was filed Tuesday, September 1, in New York federal court, backing OpenAI in the copyright suit brought by The New York Times over the use of Times content in training.
  • The national security argument states: "Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States therefore threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered." The filing cites intelligence analysis, weapon systems and battlefield recommendations including missile targeting.
  • The competition argument holds that limiting fair use would leave only the largest technology companies able to pay licensing fees, and that those fees would entrench legacy media outlets because they hold the most content AI companies want.
  • The brief argues the test is whether AI creates "significant substitutive competition" for the copyrighted work rather than whether AI causes some loss of readership, and notes the system does not give the public access to the articles it trained on.
  • It attacks the ruling in the authors' case against Meta, arguing that court improperly collapsed training and outputs into a single continuous use and adopted an indirect substitution theory based on market dilution. It urges the OpenAI court not to follow that reasoning.
  • A Times spokesperson said the administration is "siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole," and added that "AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires."
  • THR cites a 2026 study by Tuhin Chakrabarty finding book revenue fell most in the genres where AI is most prevalent.
  • Dozens of news publishers have sued AI companies over training data, and most or all of the cases will turn on fair use. Last year a federal judge rejected OpenAI's bid to dismiss core copyright claims while narrowing the case. OpenAI did not comment.

A federal film tax credit bill hits Ways and Means the week of September 14, at 20 percent of US labor costs
Insiders told TheWrap mid-November is the earliest passage. The MPA has an economic impact report due mid-September, and the DGA holds a studio side letter promising executive lobbying when the moment arrives.
CEO Summary
President Trump endorsed a federal production incentive on Truth Social on Monday after speaking with Jon Voight. Congressional insiders told TheWrap the bill will be introduced in the House Ways and Means Committee the week of September 14, with a baseline of a 20 percent credit on labor costs for productions shot in the United States. Georgia Republican Brian Jack and California Democrat Laura Friedman are expected to run point. Section 181, the only federal production credit on the books, expired at the end of 2025.
Why This Matters
Georgia and Britain won production with rebates on total production spending, so whether a credit on labor alone stacks with state programs decides how much a US shoot actually saves.
Specific Implication
Producers with a 2027 start date should have financiers price a domestic and a foreign structure in parallel now, because the credit's base and stacking rules will not be settled until the bill clears committee.
The Facts
  • The bill goes to House Ways and Means the week of September 14, after next week's recess. Details are still being negotiated. The baseline is a 20 percent tax credit on labor costs for productions shot in the United States.
  • Republicans on Ways and Means expected to be involved: Nathaniel Moran of Texas, Nicole Malliotakis of New York, Mike Carey of Ohio. Judy Chu of California is also on the committee.
  • New York raised its annual credit cap to $800 million last year. Texas raised state grant allocations to $300 million every two years through 2035. Ohio offers 30 percent on eligible spending, and Cincinnati played Metropolis in James Gunn's Superman and its sequel Man of Tomorrow.
  • Georgia production spending has fallen to a 10-year low. Marvel Studios moved Avengers production to England. Jack's district houses Trilith Studios. Friedman, a former film producer, represents Burbank.
  • Friedman said the incentive "will benefit an industry that employes 2.5 million Americans" and that she has spoken with Ways and Means Republicans from filming states.
  • Chu co-authored the CREATE Act with Malliotakis to renew and strengthen Section 181, which allowed producers to deduct up to $15 million in production spending. Introduced in August 2025, it has not been picked up. Chu notes H.R. 1 extended bonus depreciation to film and TV but the deduction cannot be taken until a production is released.
  • The MPA's economic impact report is tentatively set for mid-September, timed to the bill's introduction. The DGA and IATSE are expected to weigh in. DGA President Christopher Nolan is a potential public advocate.
  • The DGA negotiated a side letter this summer in which the studios pledged in writing to send senior executives to lobby for the incentive when deemed appropriate. The AMPTP would not name anyone.
  • Passage before the November 3 midterms is described as extremely unlikely, with mid-November the earliest realistic date. Producers and studio executives TheWrap spoke with earlier this year had not expected serious progress until 2027.
  • Canada established a national incentive 29 years ago. Britain established its program in 2007.
  • White House spokesperson Kush Desai: "President Trump has made clear his intention to protect the dominance of the American film industry."

Netflix has signed more than 20 YouTube creators and YouTube is paying its stars to stay
Netflix has signed more than 20 YouTube creators in two years, including the Stokes Twins at 145 million subscribers. YouTube is now paying its top creators to stay.

Netflix has signed deals with more than 20 YouTube creators over the past two years, plus more than 50 creator podcasts through partnerships with The Ringer, Spotify and iHeartMedia. YouTube has responded by offering incentives to its top stars to stay, on terms that vary by creator. Netflix releases creator shows the same day those creators post on YouTube. A YouTube executive drew the line for TheWrap at ownership: creators keep the IP, keep creative control and keep their own analytics. That is the term sheet, stated plainly. For a business that runs on daily audience feedback, that cost carries a number.
The Facts
  • Netflix has signed more than 20 popular YouTube creators over two years, including Alan Chikin Chow (101 million subscribers), Mark Rober (81.7 million) and Stephanie Soo (51.6 million). Recent targets include the Stokes Twins (145 million) and Nick DiGiovanni (45.5 million).
  • Separately, more than 50 creator-driven podcasts have been added through partnerships with The Ringer, Spotify and iHeartMedia.
  • At the start of last year Netflix's viewership report showed Ms. Rachel, a children's education YouTuber with 21.1 million subscribers, as the seventh most-watched show on the platform.
  • YouTube has approached top creators with retention incentives. Bloomberg and The Ankler reported more than a dozen creators took such deals; YouTube disputed those numbers. A YouTube insider said terms are "very specific" per creator.
  • Netflix's same-day-and-date strategy releases new creator shows the same day the creator posts on YouTube. That approach prompted YouTube's retention deals.
  • A Netflix insider: "We are in the talent business. We're empowering [creators] to do some of their most ambitious creative work."
  • A YouTube insider: "We're not a studio. We're not trying to become a studio. We're not owning the IP. We're not lending creative insights. Creators want to continue to maintain full control, period."
  • Netflix has historically been guarded about analytics and has no comments section. YouTube offers granular insights and direct audience contact through the YouTube Partner Program.
  • Creator content has a mixed record on the streamer: "Pop the Balloon," Colleen Ballinger's "Haters Back Off" and the Alex Cooper-produced "Let's Marry Harry" drew middling viewership.

  • MrBeast became the first YouTuber past 500 million subscribers this summer.

Jason Isbell's class action says Suno encoded artists' identities as model tokens
The complaint argues the identity right stays with the performer no matter who owns the recording copyright, and says spacing out the letters of a name defeats Suno's prompt filter.
CEO Summary
Isbell, David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Ed Calle filed a class action against Suno in Massachusetts federal court, alleging the AI music company exploits artists' identities without consent. The suit uses generated outputs as evidence. An Isbell prompt produced an Americana track called Paper Bell. A Michael Jackson prompt produced two songs called Glovebox Moonwalk, both referencing the moonwalk and a white glove. Suno says the claims are without merit and points to the prompt blocking it has in place.
Why This Matters
Right of publicity, meaning control over a person's name, voice and likeness, is state law. It does not depend on the fair use question the copyright cases against AI companies now turn on.

The framing reaches past music. A performer who has sold recordings, publishing or an entire catalog still holds the identity right unless it was licensed separately.

Proving it costs almost nothing. Type a name, save the output, file it, which is a fraction of what a copyright discovery fight runs.
Specific Implication
Catalog and library sales should address name, voice, likeness and style expressly, because a transfer of recordings alone leaves the identity right in an undefined position while it is being litigated.
The Facts
  • The suit was filed in Massachusetts federal court and obtained by Rolling Stone. Lead plaintiffs are Jason Isbell, David Lowery of Camper Van Beethoven, singer-songwriter Guy Forsyth and jazz saxophonist Ed Calle.
  • The complaint claims Suno "encoded" artists' identities into its model "without consent, and now exploits those identities" for its "considerable commercial benefit."
  • Its core framing: "Many musicians sell their rights to specific recordings. However, the identity right belongs to the performer regardless of who owns any copyright in an underlying recording unless the identity right is separately licensed, typically for merchandise under the artist's control."
  • Cited outputs: an Isbell prompt produced Paper Bell, described as "contemporary Americana singer-songwriter with fingerpicked acoustic guitar," with art showing a paper bell against a church and trees. A Buddy Guy prompt produced Stone Blues in My Shoes, described as "vintage electric Chicago blues." A Carly Simon prompt produced a song described as "soft 70s confessional pop." A Less Than Jake prompt produced Parking Lot Anthem with art the suit says invoked the band's actual cover style.
  • On filter evasion: prompting Common's legal name, Lonnie Rashid Lynn, allegedly produced tracks capturing his "more poetic, reflective, socially conscious hip-hop." Adding spaces between letters allegedly works for Taylor Swift, Bad Bunny and Bruno Mars. "m i c h a e l j a c k s o n" produced two songs called Glovebox Moonwalk, both described as "1980s pop-funk dance track[s]" with a photo of a white glove.
  • As of Rolling Stone's publication, Paper Bell and many of the other generated songs were still available on Suno.
  • Suno's statement: "We believe these claims are without merit and we intend to defend against them. Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone's name."
  • Suno CEO Mikey Shulman wrote last month that the platform has "never allowed prompts for specific artists or copyrighted songs" and redirects such prompts "toward descriptive musical characteristics."
  • Coverage of the filing reports 17 claims spanning state right-of-publicity statutes including New York, California and Tennessee, plus California common law and Illinois biometric privacy law, with allegations that Suno stored biometric voiceprints without consent.

Library licensing priced as a share of ad revenue carries more downside at a buyer moving inventory to a free tier than a flat license fee does.

CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance has asked a federal court in Oakland to require the twelve states challenging its $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, plus the Writers Guild of America, to post a $1.88 billion bond as a condition of the standstill keeping the deal from closing. The plaintiffs filed their opposition Monday, arguing that Paramount proposed and negotiated that standstill itself. Trial is set for March 2, 2027.
Why This Matters
Rule 65 security, the money a plaintiff posts in case an injunction proves to have been wrongly granted, is normally carried by private parties. The plaintiffs' brief describes the request as an attempt to "extract" money "from the public and a non-profit labor union."

The target is participation. A guild facing nine-figure exposure for joining a merger challenge has reason to appear as a friend of the court next time rather than as a plaintiff, and every future studio defendant benefits from that.
Specific Implication
Guild and union counsel weighing intervention in a studio transaction should watch the September 24 ruling for whether a court will price delay against a public enforcer at all.
The Facts
  • Motion: $1.88 billion bond against California, New York, ten other state attorneys general, and the Writers Guild of America.
  • Hearing: September 24, before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, U.S. District Court, Oakland.
  • Case filed July 13, 2026. Trial set for March 2, 2027.
  • Plaintiffs' opposition, filed Monday: "Defendant Paramount Skydance seeks to extract $1.88 billion from the public and a non-profit labor union to underwrite the costs of two private contracts it entered willfully, with advice of counsel, and for its own benefit."
  • Plaintiffs also argue Paramount cannot show the court acted "improvidently" in signing a stipulation "which Paramount itself proposed, negotiated, and then presented to this Court for signature."
  • Plaintiffs' alternative: "if the Court grants Paramount's motion, it should impose a nominal bond of $10,000."
  • Paramount spokesperson: "The Clayton Act and Rule 65 are clear: plaintiffs seeking to block a transaction must post a bond to protect against the harm caused if their challenge ultimately fails."
  • Claimed harm includes a $7 million-a-day ticking fee owed to WBD shareholders beginning at the end of September, plus potential regulatory and break-up costs.
  • A separate petition from the Iowa and Montana attorneys general asking the Supreme Court to halt the twelve states, seeking an October hearing, remains undecided.
  • Reporting places an October 1 marker on settlement talks, with David Ellison said to be weighing Texas, Georgia or Tennessee for relocation. Rob Bonta has called the relocation talk "blackmail" and accused Paramount of leaks that scuttled an August 24 settlement meeting.
  • A second Los Angeles County Department of Economic Opportunity report in two months projects large layoffs, billions in wages and hundreds of millions in tax revenue lost if the merger closes.

Apple's entertainment decisions are made a level below the chief executive, and that level is where the change happened this week. Unsealed Murdoch testimony shows Fox and News Corp executives working inside the family trust fight
Fox's chief operating officer and News Corp's chief executive attended early meetings, Fox security vetted candidate trust directors, and Bank of America was asked to model family discord as a corporate risk.
CEO Summary
More than 19,000 pages of unredacted testimony and exhibits from the Murdoch family trust case are now public. A Nevada probate commissioner had rejected Rupert Murdoch's attempt to guarantee Lachlan Murdoch permanent control of the company, and the family settled last year, with James, Elisabeth and Prudence each receiving roughly $1.1 billion to give up their interests. The trial testimony was taken in a closed Reno courtroom in September 2024.
Why This Matters
The trust's amendment power was conditioned on a good-faith finding that a change served the beneficiaries. Commissioner Edmund Gorman Jr. found the opposite, ruling that preserving trust value was "a tangential benefit rather than a true purpose." What supplied that finding was the controlling shareholder's own answer under cross-examination, agreeing that a sale to buyers with the wrong politics would diminish his legacy "regardless of the price."

Control provisions in family media holdings are therefore testable against what the controllers actually did, and the evidence that decides them is contemporaneous: meeting attendance, vetting instructions, a bank's assignment, a recording made in the room.
Specific Implication
Counsel structuring or challenging a family-controlled media trust should assume every internal step becomes discoverable, including who attended which meeting and which bank was asked what.
The Facts
  • The unsealed record runs more than 19,000 pages of unredacted testimony and exhibits. The trust amendment effort was internally named "Project Family Harmony."
  • Fox chief operating officer John Nallen and News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson attended early Project Family Harmony meetings. Fox security personnel vetted prospective replacement managing directors of the entity controlling the trust. Thomson asked Bank of America to prepare an analysis premised on family discord disrupting corporate strategy, including editorial policy.
  • The filings show the trust amendment overlapped with the aborted effort to recombine Fox Corp and News Corp.
  • Gorman found the managing directors had been "roped into a scheme" to neutralize James Murdoch because Rupert Murdoch wanted to preserve his political and editorial legacy.
  • Rupert Murdoch, then 93, testified: "Lachlan, I think, is by far the best person to run the company." He called James "very bright" but someone who "time and again showed poor judgment," and explained his delay on succession: "I was just weak."
  • Cross-examined by Gary Bornstein, he agreed that a sale of Fox and News Corp "to people with the wrong politics would diminish your legacy," regardless of price. Gorman called him the "least coached (and perhaps least coachable)" witness and among the more credible.
  • Lachlan Murdoch on the brothers' 2015 joint leadership of 21st Century Fox: "It was a disaster from day one." Rupert cited outside confusion, saying the National Football League asked "Who do we talk to? Which one?"
  • On the Disney sale, James testified Lachlan opposed it and warned "I wouldn't have a brother." Lachlan testified he brought Comcast into the auction, which by his calculation forced Disney to raise its offer by roughly $20 billion.
  • Every sibling except James gave Rupert $50 million after the Disney sale.
  • The record shows Lachlan and Siobhan McKenna set Project Family Harmony in motion before Rupert was brought in. Under cross by Lauren Moskowitz, Lachlan acknowledged no proof James leaked to an unauthorized biography or to the Financial Times, while McKenna had spent more than 14 hours with the biographer. Asked "Are you going to fire her?" he said "No." McKenna resigned from News Corp a month after the case settled.
  • Elisabeth Murdoch secretly recorded the December 2023 meeting where the amendment was unveiled, saying there: "If you think that's harmony, we must be in North Korea." She testified she skipped her father's 2024 wedding: "I found it too painful. I felt very betrayed."

Letterboxd's Bankers Are Shopping It at $250 Million to Netflix, Sony, Paramount and Private Equity
Letterboxd has about 26 million users and still cannot monetize them. Tiny bought it at a $50 million valuation in 2023, and its bankers are now seeking $250 million.
CEO Summary
Bankers at LionTree have taken meetings with Netflix, Sony Pictures, Paramount, TPG and RedBird about a sale at a potential $250 million valuation. Tiny owns about 60 percent of the company. Conversations are moving along with no frontrunner and no deal close to done, according to sources familiar with the discussions. Versant, whose CEO Mark Lazarus already holds Rotten Tomatoes and Fandango, is named as a sleeper bidder. Consultant Lauren Zeinfeld published a report last week arguing the platform could be worth a billion dollars on its data assets.
Why This Matters
Roughly one percent of a social platform's users create most of its content, and on Letterboxd that one percent is the asset being priced. Zeinfeld's framing is that the audience sits in the supply chain rather than at the end of it: "they are what produces the value instead of being the value." That makes the purchase price and the churn risk the same variable, which is what separates the Instagram outcome from the Tumblr one. Yahoo paid $1.1 billion for Tumblr in 2013 and it sold for about $3 million six years later.
Specific Implication
A buyer acquires viewing-intent data on every distributor's titles, not only its own, so a neutral holder like Versant would be a different outcome for the rest of the market than a Netflix or Sony purchase.
The Facts
  • Matthew Belloni first reported the sale exploration in July. Puck discloses that TPG and RedBird are investors in Puck.
  • Letterboxd was founded 15 years ago by Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow. Tiny acquired it in 2023 at a $50 million valuation.
  • Zeinfeld on monetization risk: "If the buyer treats the audience as an advertising surface, the critics and cinephiles who produce the highest-signal content will walk first."
  • In May, screenwriter Elizabeth Joyce launched Intrinsic Entertainment, a public benefit company, to crowdfund a community purchase.
  • Per Semafor, Tiny approached The Ankler about a sale in 2025 and could not agree terms.
  • Whip Media shut down TV Time, a comparable community app, last month despite its ratings and genre data.
  • Microsoft paid $7.5 billion for GitHub in 2018 and later launched Copilot. GitHub developers filed a class action in late 2022 arguing their free labor was extracted and resold to them; the case awaits a Ninth Circuit decision.
  • Amazon paid $55 million for IMDb in 1998 and acquired Goodreads in 2013.

The federal film tax credit has a bill name, and Canada's actors are pressing Ottawa to respond
Drafting is underway on the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a day after Jon Voight and producer Steven Paul made the case at the White House.
CEO Summary
The proposed U.S. federal production incentive now has a name and active drafting behind it, and will be framed as a jobs bill to attract Republican support. More than 120 countries offer production subsidies. The United Kingdom drew roughly $7.8 billion in inward international film and television spending in 2025, with U.S. production spending there up almost 30 percent year over year, according to the British Film Commission.
Why This Matters
Nothing has been introduced, and rival jurisdictions are already repricing. ACTRA's national office and its Toronto branch both issued statements on Tuesday, one asking Ottawa to fund Canadian production and the other asking Ontario to raise its provincial credit. Subsidy competition responds to announced intent rather than to enacted law, which means the planning risk for a 2027 or 2028 production budget starts now, before anyone knows the American credit's rate, cap or eligibility.
Specific Implication
Producers setting 2027 territory assumptions should avoid locking rebate-dependent budgets. A U.S. federal credit would change where the rebate sits in the recoupment waterfall, the order in which money is paid back, and who captures it.
The Facts
  • Bill name: the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. Trump said it has "great bipartisan response and support in Congress" and posted Tuesday: "We will bring this once great industry BACK TO AMERICA."
  • Work to craft the bipartisan bill is underway. It will be framed as a jobs initiative, on the argument that runaway production affects Republican constituencies too.
  • The push followed a Monday White House meeting between Trump and Jon Voight, Hollywood's designated "special ambassador," with Steven Paul and Scott Karol. Paul cited a film he is producing about Richard Nixon's early years that would need to shoot abroad without a federal incentive.
  • Trump was presented with other options last year, including infrastructure support and workforce development. He preferred tariffs but never imposed them. Voight, the unions and the Motion Picture Association have since pushed him toward a tax credit.
  • The United Kingdom is the current tentpole hub and hosts Marvel Studios, which left Georgia. "The Odyssey," "Jurassic World Rebirth" and "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms" shot there.
  • ACTRA national president Eleanor Noble: "It's now more important than ever, that Canada keeps its focus on producing more Canadian stories here at home."
  • ACTRA Toronto president Kate Ziegler: "If Ontario wants to remain a world-class production centre, we need a balanced plan to attract international investment, grow Canadian production and protect performers."
  • ACTRA warned of two outcomes absent stronger domestic support: American productions staying home, "hollowing out our production ecosystem," or Canada becoming "increasingly dependent on a single foreign client."
  • Pressure on Ontario's credit dates to early 2025, when British Columbia raised its incentive and New Jersey introduced one of the most generous U.S. state programs.
  • Canada and U.S. trade talks were abandoned in late August. Prime Minister Mark Carney said U.S. negotiators objected to French-language digital-content rules affecting Quebec, which he called an attack on Canadian culture and identity.

The venture money coming to Hollywood is going to microdramas, adtech and space cameras
ReelShort is reportedly on pace for $1 billion in 2026 revenue and DramaBox raised $100 million in seed funding this year.
CEO Summary
The Ankler surveyed venture investors active around entertainment and named eight firms, including CAA's Connect Ventures, Todd Boehly's Elysian Park, Alexis Ohanian's Seven Seven Six and Edgar Bronfman Jr.'s Waverly Capital. Private equity investors target an 18 to 20 percent annual return. Venture investors target 10x at the earliest stages and 3x to 5x by Series B. Seed positions can run seven to 10 years.
Why This Matters
Adam Lilling of PLUS Capital states the pricing rule directly: a star who brings "distribution, audience and trust" changes the economics enough to attract institutional capital, and the same pitch without that platform does not.

That makes an owned audience a balance-sheet asset with an observable clearing price, valued by the same investors who will not fund a content studio on its own.

The money is going to the commercialization layer rather than the content layer, which is where Hallstone Ventures put four of its first checks.
Specific Implication
A client weighing a company launch should test the pitch against Will Ward's two screens, what AI can do to the business and what a recession does to it, before approaching venture capital.
The Facts
  • Investors interviewed: Will Ward (founder, Fourward; previously at CAA and WME), Seth Hallen (founder and managing partner, Hallstone Ventures), Adam Lilling (founder and managing partner, PLUS Capital).
  • Returns: private equity targets 18 to 20 percent annually. Venture targets 10x at the earliest stages, 3x to 5x at Series B, C and D. One investor: "In venture, if something really works out, 100x is a possibility."
  • Horizons: seed investments can run seven to 10 years and beyond; growth-stage four to six. At seed, lead investors typically want double-digit ownership.
  • On IPOs, one investor: "People are chasing AI stories and almost exclusively AI stories."
  • Lilling: "Venture capital invests in platforms that scale. You might find a venture capitalist who loves movies and will write a personal check, but I don't see many VC firms backing content studios."
  • Lilling on the exception: "If Zendaya wants to start a studio, capital will show up ... partly because she brings distribution, audience and trust that genuinely change the economics of a business."
  • Hallstone's first fund was oversubscribed at $11.2 million against a $10 million goal, deployed into Orbes (cinema drones for space), Rex (adtech), Wide Worlds (fan-generated content) and Waffle Video (user-generated content for AI training). Four more are in diligence, 15 to come.
  • Hallen on the gap: "There's more content than ever before and more creators. What hasn't caught up is the ability for the commercialization of all of that content. That's still built on the old stack."
  • Ward's screens on every deal: "What can AI do to this?" and "What happens in a recession with this?" On timing: "Anything I'm going to right now is two or three years away from an exit."
  • The eight firms: CAA's Connect Ventures (Nicole Quinn, Mike Blank; spun out of the CAA and New Enterprise Associates joint venture in January); Elysian Park (Cole Van Nice; founded by Dodgers owners including Todd Boehly; checks of $500,000 to $100 million); Imaginary Ventures (Natalie Massenet, Nick Brown); Lightspeed Venture Partners (Ravi Mhatre); Seven Seven Six (Alexis Ohanian); Waverly Capital (Edgar Bronfman Jr., Daniel Leff; limited partners include Amazon, Disney, HBO, NBCUniversal and Roku); Wonder Ventures (Dustin Rosen).

Blair Levin of New Street Research locates the cost of the AT&T case in the 20 months it consumed rather than in the verdict. Paramount's version runs on a meter: roughly $7 million a day to Warner shareholders once September 30 passes.

Levin names a second cost that no fee schedule captures. Studios and other assets cannot make deals "while no one is certain who will be in charge when the deals go into production."

Martinez-Olguin has already closed the argument that carried AT&T, writing that she "cannot accept" Paramount's claim of streaming efficiencies. That leaves market definition and barriers to entry.

Anything signed at Warner Bros. before a spring ruling should price continuity of the executive relationship and approval chain across a possible change of ownership.

Every extension restores each holder's withdrawal right, so the 66.28 and 75.48 percent are a running poll of bondholder patience that resets rather than committed capital.

Anyone pricing Warner paper against a near-term settlement is pricing a date Paramount has said in its own release it does not control.

The FTC and 22 states sued Amazon over ad auction prices, alleging more than $20 billion in overcharges
The complaint says Amazon began secretly manipulating auction results in 2018 using a hidden surcharge and artificial bids. Almost half of the 1.2 million affected advertisers were small or medium-sized businesses.
CEO Summary
The Federal Trade Commission and 22 state attorneys general sued Amazon on Monday in the Western District of Washington, alleging it deceived advertisers by inflating prices in its ad auctions. The complaint covers sponsored products, brands and display ads sold against retail search results. Amazon said it strongly disagrees, calling the suit misguided and saying the claim "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate."
Why This Matters
This is the FTC's third major suit against Amazon and the first aimed at how the ad auction itself sets a price.

Amazon's own defense concedes the mechanics are opaque to buyers. It argues advertisers "adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," which is a claim that disclosure does not matter because outcomes discipline spend.

Emarketer's Zak Stambor told CNN that "Amazon is incredibly hard to walk away from." Advertisers who believe they were overcharged still have to keep buying while the case runs.
Specific Implication
Media buyers who have run Amazon campaigns since 2018 fall inside the group the complaint describes, and the restitution the FTC seeks would be calculated against auction records Amazon holds.
The Facts
  • The Federal Trade Commission and 22 state attorneys general sued Amazon on Monday, August 31, 2026, in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington.
  • The complaint alleges Amazon "likely illegally extracted over 20 billion dollars" from 1.2 million advertising customers. Almost half were small or medium-sized businesses.
  • Alleged mechanism: "in 2018, Amazon began secretly manipulating its auction results to increase its ad prices," through a hidden surcharge and artificial bids.
  • Amazon's ad auction is second-price: the winning advertiser is supposed to pay one cent more than the second-place bid.
  • The suit covers sponsored products, sponsored brands and display advertisements sold against search results on Amazon's retail site.
  • The FTC and states allege violations of federal and state consumer protection statutes and seek civil penalties, restitution and additional relief.
  • The complaint says the higher costs were eventually passed down to Amazon shoppers.
  • Amazon's response, a roughly 3,000-word statement to CNN, says it "strongly disagrees" with the "misguided" lawsuit: "The FTC's claim fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate. Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics."
  • Amazon added that even accepting the FTC's premise, it estimates advertisers "saved over $8 billion from 2021 to 2025 as a result of Amazon prioritizing ad relevancy over selecting ads on bid price alone." Amazon says it shared data with the FTC "on multiple occasions."
  • Amazon became the third-biggest ad platform in the United States in 2018.
  • Emarketer principal analyst Zak Stambor: "Advertisers face a tough challenge because Amazon is incredibly hard to walk away from." Emarketer puts Amazon's 2026 worldwide retail ecommerce sales at $927.82 billion.
  • University of Notre Dame marketing professor Vamsi Kanuri told CNN that auction-based ad buying "relies entirely on platforms strictly adhering to well-established rules."
  • Prior FTC matters: a $2.5 billion settlement last year over Prime enrollment practices ($1 billion civil penalty plus $1.5 billion in refunds to about 35 million customers), and a settlement of more than $30 million in 2023 over Alexa and Ring privacy claims. Amazon denied wrongdoing in both.
  • This is the FTC's third major lawsuit against Amazon.

Variety reported Monday that leading agencies now treat Peacock's Love Island USA as a talent pipeline, with UTA, Gersh and WME all signing from recent seasons. Contestants leave the villa under a one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities they can take, which the reporting says usually keeps them inside NBCUniversal. Peacock viewership doubled at Season 6 and has grown since.
Why This Matters
Attention on a contestant peaks at the finale and decays from there. A twelve-month hold captures that peak for NBCUniversal, and that window, more than the show itself, is what the format monetizes.

Gersh's Jade Sherman described the counterparty position directly: the franchise "tries really hard to protect their IP," and "it's on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are." Representation is being priced against terms the platform sets and revises.
Specific Implication
Agents weighing a reality-format signing should read the exclusivity term before the follower count. UTA's Jamie Youngentob said Bryce Alakai was attractive for a DJ career that predated the show, which is the asset the window does not cover.
The Facts
  • Season 8 of Love Island USA drew 19 billion minutes watched, translating to 7.9 million views, according to Peacock data cited by Variety.
  • Season 6 viewership doubled compared with previous seasons, according to NBCUniversal, and has grown in the two years since.
  • The Bravo-branded "Aftersun" spinoff, co-hosted by Summer House star Ciara Miller, saw a 135% viewership increase from last season. Other spinoffs include Beyond the Villa and Love Island Games.
  • The show is produced by ITV America and airs on Peacock. It launched on CBS in 2019 with Arielle Vandenberg hosting, moved to Peacock for Season 4 with Sarah Hyland, and Ariana Madix took over as host in Season 6.
  • Contestants leave under a one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities they can take, which Variety reports usually means keeping them inside the NBCUniversal family.
  • UTA signed Season 8 winner Bryce Alakai just over a week after the finale aired, per UTA partner and agent Mahzad Babayan.
  • Gersh represents Emmy-nominated host Ariana Madix and Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis.
  • Season 7 contestant Iris Kendall signed with WME and turned expected one-off brand deals into a full-time career.
  • UTA unscripted TV agent Jamie Youngentob: "I don't think we've seen anything quite like this. The closest thing would probably be Bravo, but those shows can take multiple seasons for somebody to really break through and stick."
  • Youngentob on why UTA signed Alakai: "He's been working incredibly hard at pursuing and building a DJ career. That was exciting for us, alongside our music colleagues." Alakai had a music career before the show and appeared in a Tubi film.
  • Gersh head of digital Jade Sherman: "Love Island is an incredible brand, and they try really hard to protect their IP. They've put things in place to do that, and it's on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are."
  • The show now connects departing Islanders with agencies and publicists, which Season 6 did not offer.
  • The finale prize is $100,000, voted on by viewers. The Season 8 reunion dropped August 31.
  • Season 6 contestant Kaylor Martin, a college senior with about 4,000 Instagram followers when she applied, is now a full-time content creator hosting her own podcast.

Summer box office stands at $4.598 billion with eight days left to beat 2013
Two films, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey, account for close to 32 percent of every ticket sold since the first Friday in May.
CEO Summary
The North American box office from the first Friday in May through August 30 stands at $4.598 billion, according to Rentrak, the second-highest summer on record behind the $4.756 billion of 2013. Eight days of the season remain through Labor Day. Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian said a like-for-like 123-day comparison would put summer 2026 at about $4.612 billion through August 31.
Why This Matters
Two titles carried a third of the season. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is about 20 percent of the summer on its own, and with The Odyssey the pair reach close to 32 percent.

That concentration is the useful number. A record-adjacent summer built on two tentpoles from Sony and Universal says the marginal dollar sits at the top of the slate, which argues for fewer and larger bets rather than a broader release calendar.
The Facts
  • Per Rentrak, the North American box office from the first Friday in May through end of day August 30 stands at $4.598 billion, the second-highest summer ever behind summer 2013's $4.756 billion.
  • The gap to the record is $158 million. Deadline reports that some sources estimate the season could come up $18 million to $22 million short.
  • The August 28-30 weekend did $100 million in the U.S. and Canada across all titles per Rentrak, up 46% over the same frame a year ago.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day took its fifth No. 1 weekend with $22.2 million.
  • Ketchup Entertainment's release of Warner Bros. Animation's Coyote vs. Acme opened to $15.4 million, the distributor's biggest opening ever, matching presales and tracking.
  • The only new major-studio wide entry next weekend is Paramount's Mark Wahlberg crime drama By Any Means. Spider-Man is forecast at $18 million to $20 million over the four-day holiday.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day is expected within days to become the second movie ever to cross $900 million domestic, after Star Wars: The Force Awakens, which stands at $936.66 million.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, represents around 20% of the entire summer's business. With Universal's The Odyssey, at $563.8 million and Christopher Nolan's highest-grossing film, the two account for close to 32% of all ticket sales from the first Friday of May through August 30.
  • Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak's Head of Marketplace Trends: "No matter where the final number lands, we have to keep the calendar in mind. There are still eight days of box office to be added from Monday, August 31 through Labor Day Monday, Sept. 7, giving this year a full 130-day summer movie season. For a true apples-to-apples comparison, the first 123 days of Summer 2026 should be compared with the 123-day summer of 2013. Based on the current forecast, Summer 2026 should stand at approximately $4.612 billion through Monday, August 31, making it the second-highest-grossing 123-day summer movie season of all time."
  • Dergarabedian: "I don't think it really matters at this point whether we beat the record. This has been such a spectacular moviegoing season that the numbers are just that and the incredible mix of films presented to audiences this year has been a game changer, not only for the industry, but for younger moviegoers."

Markiplier bought 8.5 percent of GoPro and is now its largest shareholder
GoPro is worth about $110 million, has warned it may not survive twelve months, and its largest shareholder is a YouTuber who self-released a $51 million movie.
CEO Summary
Mark Fischbach, the YouTube creator known as Markiplier, has taken an 8.5 percent stake in GoPro, making him its largest single shareholder. GoPro is valued at roughly $110 million, its shares are down more than 90 percent over five years, and the company has said there is substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. Fischbach told Bloomberg the stock looked undervalued and that he wants the company to succeed.
Why This Matters
An 8.5 percent stake in a company valued near $110 million costs under $10 million, roughly three times what Iron Lung cost to make. Fischbach said the position sits alongside an investment in Strada and is meant to push his audience toward feature production. That makes it a supply-side bet. He is buying the tools his viewers would need before they need them.
Specific Implication
A camera vendor operating under a going-concern warning is a live counterparty risk for any production standardizing on its hardware.
The Facts
  • Mark Fischbach, the YouTube creator known as Markiplier, has acquired an 8.5% stake in GoPro, making him the largest single shareholder.
  • GoPro is valued at about $110 million. Its shares are down more than 55% this year and more than 90% over the past five years.
  • GoPro said in May it was exploring strategic alternatives and has since said there is "substantial doubt about the company's ability to continue as a going concern for the next twelve months."
  • Fischbach: "I saw the stock and where it was, I was like that seems undervalued. It's just something I've been cooking in the background; I want the company to succeed."
  • He has also invested in Strada, which makes tools for transferring large files between filmmakers.
  • Fischbach is 37, has posted as Markiplier for about 15 years, and has nearly 40 million YouTube subscribers.
  • His film Iron Lung grossed $51 million on a $3 million budget and was distributed by Fischbach himself, without a major studio.
  • He used GoPro cameras for behind-the-scenes footage on Iron Lung but did not consider them good enough for principal photography.
  • That changed when he saw a teaser for GoPro's Mission 1 Pro ILS, an interchangeable-lens camera weighing 6.95 ounces that the company calls a cinema camera.
  • Fischbach attended the National Association of Broadcasters trade show in Las Vegas in April to see GoPro's next camera.
  • Fischbach: "One of the things I want to do is push my audience to the risky world of trying to make feature films and higher-end productions."

The FCC's only Democrat says she wants a second term during the Disney license review
Gomez says broadcasters now ask her whether it is safe to report on particular subjects, and that the question itself is the problem.
CEO Summary
Anna Gomez, the only Democrat on the Federal Communications Commission, told The Hollywood Reporter she wants to be renominated. Her term ended in June and she is serving a carryover period, an expired term she may hold until replaced, which could run through the end of 2027. She dissented from the agency's approval of the Paramount-Skydance merger and has publicly urged Disney to fight the FCC's early review of its broadcast licenses.
Why This Matters
Gomez can hold her seat into 2027 without another confirmation vote, and that carryover is the whole of her leverage. The White House has not said whether it will fill the two vacant seats, so a three-member commission can keep clearing transactions and opening license reviews on 2-1 party-line votes. For a broadcaster with a renewal pending, that vote count is the operative fact.
Specific Implication
Companies holding broadcast licenses should price early-renewal risk into station and network valuations, since the agency has now tied a renewal review to a company's internal policies.
The Facts
  • Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner at the Federal Communications Commission, told The Hollywood Reporter: "I'd love to be reconfirmed, and I have supporters in the Senate, which I'm very grateful for, and appreciate very much." She added: "I think it's important that we maintain somebody that pushes back against this administration's overreaches."
  • Gomez's term ended at the end of June. She is in a carryover period that could last until the end of 2027 unless another commissioner is nominated and confirmed by the Senate before then.
  • The law caps commissioners from a single party at three. The commission is typically five members and can operate with a quorum of three.
  • Gomez was appointed under President Biden in 2023 and confirmed 55-43. Republican Brendan Carr chairs the agency; Republican Olivia Trusty was named a commissioner in 2025.
  • Earlier this month President Trump nominated Carr's senior counsel, Danielle Thumann, a Republican, for a five-year commissioner term. She has not been confirmed. The President has not said whether he would fill a fifth seat or support Gomez's renomination.
  • Gomez dissented from the FCC's 2-1 approval of the Paramount-Skydance merger, which required the company to eliminate its DEI programs and put controls on newsroom decisions at CBS.
  • Last spring she launched a nationwide First Amendment tour.
  • She has been outspoken on the FCC's decision to call Disney's broadcast licenses for early renewal, which the agency tied to Disney's DEI policies and which followed administration calls for action against Jimmy Kimmel over a joke.
  • Gomez, in a May social media post: "The FCC is once again targeting an administration critic by mob rule. Let's not pretend this FCC hasn't already made up its mind. All they want is for their pro-censorship partisan allies to nod in agreement. My message to Disney: Don't flinch. Fight."
  • Gomez said she hopes she "played no small part in ensuring that Disney did stand up and sue the FCC about this retaliation."
  • Carr previously said in a hearing that "any broadcaster that complies with the public interest standard is not in any risk at all," and, pressed on retaliation, that "there is no First Amendment right to an FCC license." He also said the FCC was "not formally an independent agency."
  • Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told Punchbowl News in April: "It is not government's job to censor speech, and I do not believe the FCC should operate as the speech police."
  • Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) support Gomez's renomination and a return to a five-member bipartisan commission.
  • Gomez says broadcasters ask her whether it is safe to report on given topics: "the fact that you're asking me that question is the problem because it is not for the FCC to make your editorial decisions."
  • She warns early license renewals "devalue the licenses themselves."

John Ternus Becomes Apple CEO on September 1 With the Services Business Slowing
Tim Cook stays on as executive chairman and keeps Apple's relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government. Services chief Eddy Cue is among the executives Bloomberg reports will take on a larger role.
CEO Summary
John Ternus, Apple's hardware chief, becomes chief executive on September 1, succeeding Tim Cook after 15 years. Cook began seriously considering him as a successor two years ago. Ternus spent 25 years in hardware and is less experienced in finance, sales, legal affairs, government relations and procurement, so he will rely on other executives. Apple's revenue roughly quadrupled to $416 billion during Cook's tenure and its market value rose fifteenfold.
Why This Matters
Apple TV+ reports into services, and services is the one line Apple's own executives told Bloomberg they expect to keep decelerating. They attribute the slowdown to weak game purchases as users move to TikTok, to App Store take rates lowered under regulatory pressure, and to the EU forcing Apple to admit independent app stores. None of those causes can be fixed with better shows.

Bloomberg also reports that the heads of marketing, services and retail have each been at Apple about four decades and could retire within a few years, and that roughly half the leadership team could exit. A content commitment underwritten by a relationship with Cue now carries a shorter sponsor horizon than the deal term.
Specific Implication
Producers and representatives negotiating Apple TV+ commitments should expect approval to route through a division defending its own growth rate, and should check whether renewal or extension terms depend on a single executive relationship.
The Facts
  • John Ternus, 51, becomes CEO on September 1. Tim Cook, 65, has been CEO since 2011 and becomes executive chairman.
  • Cook has told Ternus he will keep managing Apple's relationships with President Donald Trump and the Chinese government, and has told staffers the company will remain his No. 1 priority.
  • Apple revenue roughly quadrupled to $416 billion under Cook; market value rose fifteenfold.
  • COO Sabih Khan, CFO Kevan Parekh and services chief Eddy Cue are poised for bigger roles, according to people close to the company.
  • Apple executives attribute the services slowdown to weak game purchases as users shift to TikTok and other entertainment, and project it to continue. App Store take rates have been lowered in many markets under regulatory pressure, and the EU is forcing Apple to allow independent app stores.
  • Apple cut Vision Pro jobs. The cuts were mostly centered on gaming and immersive video content, and, in a previously unreported move, also hit device security, audio engineering, Siri integration, testing and the operating system.
  • Ternus never truly supported the Vision Pro, per people who discussed it with him, but does support the non-augmented-reality smart glasses code-named N50 planned for next year.
  • The heads of marketing, services and retail have each been at Apple about four decades. People close to the company say roughly half the leadership team could exit in the next few years.
  • Apple has sued OpenAI over alleged trade-secret theft. Hundreds of former Apple employees work in OpenAI's hardware division. Ternus was among the executives who greenlit the suit.
  • Cook's farewell dinner was held at Apple Park on August 23.

Universal Is the First Studio Past $3 Billion Internationally This Year, on The Odyssey

CEO Summary
Universal crossed $3 billion at the international box office in 2026, the first studio to reach the mark this year, pushed over by Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. The film stands at $1.55 billion worldwide in its seventh weekend. Universal had already become the first studio to pass $4 billion worldwide this year. An original screenplay carried Universal across a threshold reached three times in seven years, and premium large format (the biggest and brightest auditorium tier) has produced close to 30% of the film's worldwide gross.

Phil Tippett has closed the Berkeley visual effects studio he ran for four decades, auctioning stop-motion models, cameras, fabrication equipment and production material. Why This Matters
Tippett Studio kept the work and sold the building. Specific Implication
Productions planning practical, stop-motion or motion-control sequences should book physical capacity at contracting rather than assume the vendor holds it in house.

  • From the company's statement: "Stop-motion remains an important part of our creative capabilities, but maintaining a large permanent physical footprint is no longer necessary for our current requirements. CEO Summary
The two publishers filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. They seek up to $150,000 per infringed work plus up to $25,000 for each instance in which copyright management information was stripped, which the filing puts in the billions at the maximum award. The complaint alleges Mann used BitTorrent to download more than five million pirated books and that employees took at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror. MusixMatch and LyricFind already pay these publishers to license the same lyrics. If Anthropic pulled the text from those two services rather than from the open web, the publishers can put an established market price on precisely what was taken. A demonstrated price is the evidence a fair use defense handles worst, because it converts an abstract argument about transformation into a number the defendant declined to pay.
Specific Implication
Catalog owners licensing to lyric and metadata services should check whether those agreements bar downstream AI ingestion. The complaint points at the licensee as the leak point.

California Carves Independent Film Out of Its New $5 Million Tax Credit Cap; Studios Get a Faster Cash Refund Instead
Independent film accounts for 10% of the $750 million program and gets the only full exemption. Studios instead get their cash refund in two years at a 5% discount, down from five years at 10%.
CEO Summary
California lawmakers unveiled AB 186 on Friday evening, a trailer bill amending the state's $750 million film and TV incentive after June's Senate Bill 122 capped the tax credits any business may claim at $5 million or 70% of liability per year. Independent productions are fully exempt from that cap. Major studio productions are not, and instead get a faster, cheaper cash refund on credits they elect to monetize. Both houses must pass the bill by midnight Monday, the last day of the legislative session.
Why This Matters
Sacramento refused the full carveout the Motion Picture Association and the Entertainment Union Coalition asked for, and the stated reason is the constraint worth remembering: a film-specific exemption would have brought tech asking for the same one, which would have hollowed out SB 122. That sets the terms for every future ask. Relief that arrives inside a general business-tax vehicle can pass. Relief framed as Hollywood's alone runs into an argument about who else is in line.
Specific Implication
Independent producers can again pledge an uncapped California credit to financiers. Studios should reprice their credits at a 5% discount received over two years before the next round of location decisions.
The Facts
  • AB 186 was unveiled Friday evening, August 28, 2026. It must pass both houses by midnight Monday, August 31. It is expected to pass.
  • Authored by Sen. Ben Allen and Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, who also wrote the 2025 bill raising the program from $330 million to $750 million.
  • SB 122, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on June 29, 2026, caps credits for any business at $5 million or 70% of total liability per year, whichever is greater, for three years. It was written to raise corporate tax revenue, not to target film.
  • Independent film, 10% of the $750 million program, is fully exempt from the cap. Major studio productions are not.
  • Refund election: current law gives cash instead of a credit against liability at a 10% discount over five years. AB 186 makes it a 5% discount over two years.
  • Carry-forward on credits earned under earlier program versions extends from 10 years to 15, per TheWrap. Variety describes the provision as extending the expiration of non-refundable pre-2025 credits by up to five years, protecting credits at risk of expiring after nine.
  • A provision easing claims against sales tax, sought by studios, was dropped from an earlier circulating version.
  • The MPA, the Entertainment Union Coalition and the Producers Guild of America signed on. Studio government affairs officials took part in negotiations, per TheWrap.
  • Kathleen Thompson, vice president of tax incentives at Cast & Crew: "It meaningfully improves the situation. They threw a bone to both the studios and to independents."
  • Zbur: the fix provides "greater stability and certainty" for production workers, and "does not address every challenge facing this highly competitive and mobile industry."
  • Deadline's account of the same bill calls it "AB136." Variety and TheWrap both give AB 186.

Amazon Leaked a 4K Master of Lionsgate's $50 Million Statham Film, and the Contract Chain Leaves Buyers No One to Sue
International buyers would have to sue the producers, who would then have to sue Amazon. No one wants to, so buyers are hoping for a voluntary payment instead.
CEO Summary
Amazon unintentionally leaked a 4K fully mixed master of Mutiny, a $50 million Jason Statham action film, before its Lionsgate theatrical release. The U.S. opening weekend came in under $8 million, the UK managed $500,000, and the global gross stands near $16 million. TorrentFreak lists it as the most pirated film of the week. Amazon, Lionsgate and the producers all declined to comment.
Why This Matters
Territory buyers took the loss but hold no contract with Amazon, so reaching it requires two sequential suits between parties who work together constantly. Buyers concede they cannot quantify the harm anyway, which means any remedy resting on proof of causation fails on these facts. A clause triggered by the event, unauthorized availability before the window opens, would survive where one resting on proven loss does not.
Specific Implication
On any territory license where an upstream party holds the master, buyers should ask who they can actually sue and negotiate either a direct right of action or an assignment of the producer's claim.
The Facts
  • Amazon leaked Mutiny before its theatrical run. Deadline reported the leak the previous week; this is the follow-up on impact.
  • The film is a $50 million Lionsgate release and has now opened in most territories.
  • U.S. opening weekend did not reach $8 million. The UK took $500,000. Global gross is roughly $16 million.
  • Luminate's Box Office Insider shows a $10,026,438 domestic cume through August 26, sixth on that day's chart at $580,778, down 46.2%.
  • TorrentFreak lists it as the most pirated film of the week.
  • A person close to the film: "It's very rare to get a 4K fully mixed version of a film online. It's usually a badly recorded camera version from theaters. The box office is certainly a bad surprise. Tracking ranged and the film had similar metrics to other successful Statham movies but it's running at half or less of the box office."
  • Deadline names competing explanations: the staying power of Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey, and softness in the star's recent results, noting Shelter also underwhelmed.
  • A buyer: "There's no way the leak cost people zero. It's hard to know if it cost hundreds of dollars or millions in each territory but it's clearly being streamed globally."
  • Per lawyers consulted by interested parties, the chain of title means international buyers would have to sue the producers, who would have to sue Amazon. Deadline reports little appetite for litigation.
  • An overseas buyer: "There has been a lot of finger-pointing. What Amazon did was totally unacceptable. But no one is taking a lead on it internationally."
  • Buyers hope Amazon offers what is described as "the good-faith thing," some voluntary compensation. Nothing obliges it to.
  • Statham is understood to be among those disappointed. Lionsgate is in talks with Amazon and is still assessing impact. Premium VOD numbers are expected to clarify the picture.

A Third of Cord-Cutters Buy a Streaming Plan Within a Month, and Most Pick Ad-Free
Six of the ten plans cord-cutters bought first were ad-free, led by Paramount+ Premium at 13.7%. Their income distribution matched the general population almost exactly.
CEO Summary
Antenna found that 31% of traditional cord-cutters signed up for a new streaming service within a month of canceling pay TV in the first quarter, five times the normal rate. Six of the top ten plans they chose were ad-free. Separately, average churn across the major streamers was 4% in July, ranging from Netflix at 2% to Peacock and Starz at 7%.
Why This Matters
Paramount+ Premium takes the largest share of first-month sign-ups and carries the highest churn of the majors at 6%, which is an acquisition win sitting on top of a retention problem. The income data closes off the obvious explanation: 61% of cord-cutters earn under $100,000, and so does 61% of the general population. These households dropped pay TV and then paid up for ad-free streaming, which points at packaging rather than price.
The Facts
  • 31% of traditional cord-cutters signed up for a new streaming service within a month of canceling in Q1 2026, five times the normal sign-up rate, per Antenna.
  • Top ten first-month plans by share: Paramount+ Premium 13.7%, Netflix Premium 11.5%, Peacock Premium 9.5%, Netflix Standard 9.5%, Netflix Standard With Ads 9.3%, Apple TV Standard 8.5%, Starz Standard 7.1%, Paramount+ Essential 7%, Hulu Standard 6.7%, Disney+ Duo Basic 6.6%.
  • 72% of traditional cord-cutters already held at least one premium SVOD subscription before canceling. For those leaving virtual pay TV services such as YouTube TV or Sling TV, that figure was 84%.
  • Of those who canceled pay TV between January 2024 and March 2026, 61% had household income of $100,000 or less, the same share as the general population. Households above $200,000 were 13% of cord-cutters versus 12% of the general population.
  • July churn: Netflix 2%, Disney+ 3%, Discovery+ and Hulu 4%, Apple TV and HBO Max 5%, Paramount+ 6%, Starz 7%, Peacock 7%. Category average 4%.

Audio Rights Are Being Pulled Out of Book Deals and Priced Separately
Active audiobook titles grew 43% in 2025 while revenue grew 9%. Literary agent Kimberly Brower says advances have not moved anywhere near as much as sales would suggest.
CEO Summary
More than 750,000 audiobook titles were active in 2025, up 43% year over year, while U.S. audiobook revenue grew 9% to $2.43 billion, per the Audio Publishers Association. Audio rights that publishers once bundled into print deals without a separate price now draw competing bids from publishers, audio-first companies, podcast studios and platforms including Spotify and Amazon's Audible. Two named sources, one on the producer side and one on the agent side, describe the same shift.
Why This Matters
Pushkin's Eric Sandler says there are now "real comps, and competition amongst bidders" on a right that five years ago went across with print at no stated value. Brower, who sits on the other side of that negotiation, says the money has not followed: audiobooks have "not moved the needle as much as one would think given how high audiobook sales have gotten."

Both statements can be true, and together they describe a right whose market price is rising faster than its negotiated price. That gap is the whole opportunity, and it stays open only until the bundling default breaks.
Specific Implication
Where a client's underlying literary property is being optioned, the audio right should be priced in that negotiation rather than assumed to have traveled with the print deal.
The Facts
  • More than 750,000 audiobook titles were active in 2025, up 43% from 2024, per the Audio Publishers Association. U.S. audiobook revenue grew 9% to $2.43 billion, slowing from 13% growth in 2024.
  • 58% of American adults, an estimated 157 million people, have listened to an audiobook, up from 51% or roughly 134 million a year earlier.
  • Eric Sandler, chief strategy officer at Pushkin Industries: "In publishing, audio has gone from being the piece nobody negotiated, and many still don't, to what can amount to an incredibly impactful part of the deal."
  • Sandler on the bidder set: publishers, audio-first companies, podcast studios and distribution platforms, with Spotify moving deeper into audiobooks alongside Audible.
  • Sandler on where leverage sits: "Leverage, meanwhile, follows the audience. Authors who bring listeners with them continue to have a leg up."
  • Kimberly Brower, founding partner and CEO of Park, Fine & Brower Literary Management, said audio has gone from something publishers wanted to control to something they "need to have."
  • Asked whether audiobooks have produced larger advances or higher valuations, Brower said sometimes, "but I have not seen it move the needle as much as one would think given how high audiobook sales have gotten."

Fandango distributed its first film, the faith-based concert picture House of Worship, in about 400 theaters last weekend for a three-day run.   • On the parent: "Linear cable is obviously a challenged business but it spins off a lot of cash." Golf Channel went from 85% of revenue to roughly 50/50 after Golf Now and Golf Pass were built. Versant plans the same across CNBC, MS NOW, and E!/USA Sports Network.
  • On exhibitors: "I don't view [other programs] as competitive at all. I want to sell their loyalty programs." Fandango waives fees for a circuit's loyalty members when the circuit does. "I don't ever want to be viewed as a competitor."

If Bonta Forces Paramount to Sell Cable Networks, the Analyst View Is That Almost No One Wants Them
Disney's A+E stake went at 4 times EBITDA. Paramount has been trying to sell BET for about five years. Comcast shuttered low-rated networks rather than sell them.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is pushing Paramount to divest cable networks as a condition of settling the antitrust case stalling its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. Scott Robson, senior research analyst at S&P Global Market Intelligence's Kagan group, told TheWrap the likely buyers are private equity and broadcast station groups, and that even those are hard to find: "It's hard to find a buyer for a depreciating asset." Bloomberg Intelligence estimates CNN, TBS and TNT could fetch roughly $8 billion together.
Why This Matters
The remedy may not be performable. Comcast's choice to shutter networks rather than sell them is a company revealing it valued those assets below the cost of a transaction, and Paramount's five-year failure to move BET says the same thing from the seller's side. Robson also raises the question a divestiture order would have to answer and usually does not: whether a sale conveys the linear feed alone or the content library behind it. Those are different assets, with different buyers and different prices.
Specific Implication
Anyone valuing a linear network should work from the 4x EBITDA A+E mark and confirm whether the backlog travels with the channel before pricing it.
The Facts
  • Talks between Paramount and the state attorneys general are in limbo. Bonta is pushing for divestiture of some combined-company networks.
  • Sector figures cited by Robson: cable network ad revenue down 10% year to date against 2025; carriage fee revenue down 3%; pay-TV subscriptions down from a 2012 peak above 100 million to roughly 60 million this year including virtual MVPDs such as YouTube TV. Citing a survey of homes keeping cable for sports, he said subscribers could fall another 30%.
  • Valuation marks: Disney's A+E Global Networks stake sold at 4 times EBITDA. Hearst bought Disney's 50% of A+E Global Media for $1.2 billion earlier this month. Bloomberg Intelligence puts CNN, TBS and TNT at roughly $8 billion combined.
  • Named potential buyers: private equity, plus broadcast station owners Hearst, Nexstar Media Group (The CW, NewsNation), E.W. Scripps (Ion) and Byron Allen's Allen Media Group (The Weather Channel).
  • On CNN: Barry Diller has expressed interest should it be for sale, and former CNN CEO Jeff Zucker, now at RedBird Capital, might bid. But Paramount CEO David Ellison wrote a New York Times op-ed this month asserting CNN ownership is at the heart of the merger challenges, and denied interest in selling it.
  • Robson on why Paramount holds: despite falling ratings, CNN and TNT generate the cash flow needed to pay down debt from the WBD purchase.
  • Robson: "Are they going to sell just the rights to the linear feed, or are they going to sell the entire backlog of content? Because those are two very different business models."
  • The expected roll-up never happened. After Comcast's 2024 and WBD's 2025 spinoff announcements, Netflix bid for WBD's streaming and studio assets but not its cable properties, and Versant said it wants linear below 50% of revenue.
  • Robson on Comcast shuttering networks: "It's like deeming them worthless."
  • In the same column's Deal Sheet: Arctos, a KKR-owned private equity firm, bought 10% of the Atlanta Falcons at a $10.6 billion valuation, its fourth NFL stake. Marc Shad agreed to buy control of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx at a $4.5 billion valuation. DAZN is acquiring EverPass Media, holder of NFL Sunday Ticket commercial rights, terms undisclosed.
