'Coyote vs. Acme' Opens Friday, Three Years After Warner Took a $30 Million Write-Off on It
Netflix, Amazon and Paramount all bid for the shelved film. Producer Chris DeFaria says Warner Bros. turned the offers down and would not let the bidders counter.
CEO Summary
"Coyote vs. Acme" opens in theaters Friday through Ketchup Entertainment, three years after Warner Bros. Discovery declared the completed film would not be released and took a $30 million tax write-off on it. The studio had done the same with a nearly finished "Batgirl" and the almost-complete "Scoob! Holiday Haunt." Producer Chris DeFaria and star Will Forte spoke to TheWrap about the period between.
Why This Matters
DeFaria draws the line where it belongs: studios abandon projects often, "but it's very unusual that that kind of process would govern a film that's finished. I've never seen that before in my life. That's the real change." Delivery used to be the point at which a filmmaker's exposure ended.

The resale detail is the sharper one. Offers came in from Netflix, Amazon and Paramount, the last with a theatrical component, and Warner declined them without permitting counters. A write-off is worth more to the owner than a sale only if no sale is allowed to establish a price.
Specific Implication
Release-obligation and reversion language should be tested against the case where a picture is complete and the owner declines to release or to sell, since that is now a documented outcome rather than a hypothetical.
The Facts
  • "Coyote vs. Acme" opens in theaters Friday, August 28, distributed by Ketchup Entertainment.
  • In November 2023 Warner Bros. Discovery said the film was fully completed but would not be released, shelving it for a $30 million tax write-off.
  • The studio previously shelved a nearly finished "Batgirl" and canceled the almost-complete animated "Scoob! Holiday Haunt."
  • DeFaria: "It was ordered by one regime at the studio and inherited by another. That's always rocky."
  • DeFaria: "It's very unusual that that kind of process would govern a film that's finished. I've never seen that before in my life. That's the real change."
  • After public outcry Warner pledged to shop the film. TheWrap reported in early 2024 that Warner executives called DeFaria wanting it off the books. Offers arrived from several studios and streamers including Netflix and Amazon, and Paramount proposed an ambitious theatrical component. Warner declined the offers and would not allow counters.
  • Forte: "It was confusion first. It cycled through a lot of stuff, a lot of confusion, which turned into just rage for a long time, and then just sorrow."
  • Forte, after a "funeral screening" on the Warner lot: "All of us after watching that movie were looking around at each other and saying, 'Is this the version that they saw that made them want to get rid of it?'"
  • The executives who made the decision, including CEO David Zaslav, had not watched the film.
  • Adapted from Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker story. James Gunn revived it at Warner in 2015 and holds producer and "story by" credit. Dave Green directed. Shot in New Mexico in 2022 with 180 local crew, 49 local principal actors and roughly 2,120 background talent. Cast includes Forte, Lana Condor, John Cena, Luis Guzmán and Eric Bauza. VFX and animation by DNEG.

Top Gun got 19 million, Avatar 14 million, Titanic 13 million. The Encore trailer carries an exclusive look at Avengers: Doomsday, which opens December 18.

The trailer for Avengers Endgame: Encore recorded 77 million views in its first 24 hours, more than four times any previous re-release trailer, per Deadline. The film returns to theaters September 25 with an exclusive Avengers: Doomsday look attached, and a longer sneak peek reserved for IMAX and Infinity Vision certified screens.
Why This Matters
The three prior re-release trailers cluster between 13 and 19 million, which is roughly what nostalgia on its own produces. Deadline attributes the gap largely to appetite for the new Doomsday footage, which makes the re-release an advertising placement that also sells tickets. Gating the longer peek behind premium formats routes audiences there four months before the tentpole opens. One caution on the number itself: 77 million is a supplied count with no platform breakdown or view definition, so it is not strictly like-for-like against the comps.

Studios weighing a library re-release should sequence it against an upcoming title with exclusive footage attached, rather than against an anniversary.

  • The Encore presentation includes an exclusive Doomsday look. An additional sneak peek is available only on IMAX and Infinity Vision certified screens.

Which Cable Networks Ellison Would Have to Sell to Settle With Bonta
Bonta told the Ankler Agenda the remedy targets the cable portfolio rather than CNN. WBD's cable arm earned $1.45 billion in second-quarter adjusted operating profit; Paramount's earned $1.06 billion.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta told the Ankler Agenda podcast on Monday that a structural remedy, meaning a forced sale rather than a promise about conduct, would stop Paramount holding all 50 of the most sought-after US cable channels under one roof. Twelve state attorneys general are suing to block the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. The Ankler surveyed more than half a dozen veteran cable executives on which networks David Ellison would fight to keep, which he could afford to lose, and who would buy the rest.
Why This Matters
The A+E sale to Hearst cleared north of $1 billion because Hearst owns roughly forty years of its own programming. Most Paramount and WBD channels do not own theirs. Comedy Central's remaining value sits almost entirely in The Daily Show and a 50 percent stake in South Park, both of which Ellison could move to Paramount+ and strip out.

That inverts the usual order of valuation. Nielsen rank says what a channel delivers this quarter. Rights ownership says what it is worth once the carriage deals end. Private equity, the buyer class sources name first, prices the second one.
Specific Implication
A producer with a series on a WBD or Paramount cable network should establish whether the network or the parent holds the underlying rights. That determines which entity a divestiture would put across the table.
The Facts
  • Bonta: "When it comes to cable channel licensing, a structural remedy means you can't have all 50 of the most sought-after channels in the United States of America; some other entity has to have control of those. That's what it means to have a structural remedy; you can't have them under the Paramount-Warner Bros. roof."
  • WBD holds seven networks in Nielsen's top 25: TNT, HGTV, TBS, CNN, TLC, Food Network and Discovery. Paramount earns more total linear revenue, largely on CBS, the most-watched network of 2025.
  • 66.1 million US households still subscribe to cable, per Evoca.tv, down 35 percent since 2010 and down from 68.7 million a year ago. Streaming is now nearly half of television viewing.
  • Paramount would carry an estimated $80 billion in debt at close. One source: "If I sell off my predominant revenue stream, what am I left with? A studio that might make or lose a little money? Is that a business?"
  • HBO Max has 140 million subscribers; Paramount+ has 79.6 million.
  • None of the executives surveyed believed Ellison would sell CNN.
  • Sources named TruTV and VH1 as the first to go. TNT and TBS are seen as too broad next to CBS, with sports the counterargument: they share NCAA tournament rights with CBS through 2032, so a merged company would hold the whole tournament. One source: "The only reason TNT and TBS exist is for live sports."
  • Disney's sale of its 50 percent A+E Global Media stake to Hearst brought north of $1 billion. Hearst owns the bulk of that programming outright.
  • Named exceptions with owned IP: TNT produced The Last Ship and Falling Skies, both recently charting on Netflix after WBD licensed them. Comedy Central produces The Daily Show and owns 50 percent of South Park with Trey Parker and Matt Stone.
  • Prior asking prices: Paramount turned down $3 billion for Showtime in 2023; Shari Redstone weighed a $1.6 billion BET sale in 2024; Paramount sought a stake buyer for MTV in January.
  • Named potential buyers: private equity ("holds on to declining assets with high and predictable revenue and milks them until the end"), Versant, Nexstar, Hearst, and Byron Allen's Allen Media Group, which bought a majority of BuzzFeed for $120 million in May.
  • Paramount statement: "Paramount remains hopeful and is committed to good faith discussions with Attorney General Bonta's office for an efficient resolution of our pending litigation."

A producer targeting Warner Bros. film should establish whether the project routes through De Luca and Abdy or arrives above them. The reporting describes both paths operating.

Independent Theaters Want the Merger Settlement to Cover Rental Terms, Holds and Library Access
Phoenix Theaters owner Cory Jacobson wants Paramount's 30-film, 45-day commitment extended from three years to five, noting his building leases run as long as 25 years.
CEO Summary
AMC, Regal and Cinemark have endorsed the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger after David Ellison agreed to put a 30-film annual slate and a 45-day theatrical window in writing. Cinema United, the trade group representing chains of every size, wrote to Ellison and California Attorney General Rob Bonta on August 18 asking that a settlement also cover rental terms for smaller theaters, booking flexibility, marketing support and continued access to both companies' libraries. Paramount did not respond to IndieWire's request for comment.
Why This Matters
Three years is shorter than a development cycle. A commitment that expires before a film greenlit under it has finished shooting cannot be financed against, which is what Jacobson is actually asking to fix.

The precedent driving the library request is specific. After Disney closed the Fox acquisition in 2019, Home Alone, Alien and Fight Club became largely unavailable to independent exhibitors. Repertory bookings are what fill an independent's calendar between wide releases, and Paramount has not historically shared Disney's withholding policy.
The Facts
  • The three largest US chains want a steady film supply, a guaranteed 45-day theatrical exclusive window, and no prolonged legal fight. Ellison has been willing to put those promises in writing.
  • Cinema United's August 18 letter asks that the 30 annual releases be marketed and promoted in theaters of all sizes, that rental terms not rise for smaller theaters with less negotiating power, that safeguards exist for small theaters making their own booking choices, and that both libraries stay accessible.
  • An independent owner who signed the letter: "There are differences between big circuits to the smallest, and we're all providing the same product for our guests, but how we get from here to there, it's different for the independents."
  • Same owner: "Commitment to the 30 films is certainly a starting point, but there's a lot of questions that need to be worked out. How widely will they be released, how will they be marketed, and will independent theaters have reasonable access to these films?"
  • Single-screen theaters can be required to hold a film for multiple weeks on "clean screens," playing only that title across all showtimes. Terms are often set uniformly regardless of venue size, so a flop damages a single-screen operator more than a circuit spreading risk across hundreds of sites.
  • Jacobson, who runs 10 locations, supports the merger and also wants tiered terms based on how a film performs.
  • An exhibition expert called studio views on withholding library titles "short-sighted" and said that even for the major chains, "the devil is in the details."
  • A West Coast mid-size owner: "Unfortunately we don't drive the bus. I think there's always going to be a challenge for people that have less than more for people to negotiate their position." He added a settlement is "an opportunity so we don't have to take them at their word."
  • Documentary filmmakers have raised a parallel concern about archival footage licensing from a CNN under Ellison and Bari Weiss.

A Microdrama Platform Publishes Its Revenue Split and Lets Creators Keep Film and TV Rights
The split runs 70 percent to the creative team and 30 percent to the platform. Inside the creative share, directors take 30 percent and the creator or showrunner takes 20.
CEO Summary
Roy Price, the former head of Amazon Studios, launched Number One Best Website on Monday. The site hosts user-uploaded microdramas, meaning vertical serials cut into one-to-few-minute episodes, and matches collaborators. Viewers buy tokens to keep watching. Creators retain movie and television rights while the project IP can be sold separately to third parties. As of publication every microdrama on the platform appeared to be AI-generated. Owl & Co projects the sector will generate $150 billion outside China in 2026.
Why This Matters
The published split pays the director more than the showrunner, which reverses how television allocates and matches how the format is actually made. Every other US vertical platform commissions top-down and keeps the rights, so this is the first itemized number a creator can negotiate against.
Specific Implication
Anyone quoting terms on a short-form vertical deal now has a public benchmark to anchor to, including the 5 percent line for a music supervisor and the retention of film and television rights.
The Facts
  • Revenue split: 70 percent creative team, 30 percent platform. Within the creative share: 20 percent creator/showrunner, 30 percent director(s), 10 percent episode writer(s), 5 percent bible writer(s), 5 percent music supervisor.
  • Project IP can be bought by third parties; the creator retains movie and TV rights.
  • Price on the model: "The general idea is it's not a centralized system. Most of the [microdrama platforms] that exist now are centralized and top-down, like a traditional network or studio, and they're pretty narrow in terms of their genre or focus. We're the opposite of that, more like YouTube or TikTok."
  • Price on AI: video generators cannot yet make great movies but produce a "good result" for verticals.
  • Price on the market gap: "There is room for a content brand that has a different vibe that is definitely not DramaBox, but it's not even Netflix or any mainstream streamer. I think that comedy, certain kinds of action and so on are a little underserved in the main market."
  • The platform is a website only, with no app yet.
  • Price ran Amazon Studios through Transparent, Bosch and Manchester by the Sea. He resigned in 2017 facing a sexual harassment claim from Man in the High Castle executive producer Isa Hackett, which he denied.
  • Other Hollywood entrants into verticals: Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun (aTwist), Bill Block (GammaTime), Issa Rae's HOORAE, Taye Diggs (Microhouse Film), and David Oyelowo and Nate Parker (Mansa).
  • THR notes the open question: vertical companies spend heavily on show-by-show consumer acquisition while many apps compete to become the default, and production costs could rise as the sector matures.

CEO Summary
Chris Hansen told radio host Dan Abrams he hasn't decided whether to pursue legal action against A24's "Primetime," a dramatization starring Robert Pattinson as Hansen that adapts an Esquire article about a fatal "To Catch a Predator" sting. Hansen disputes A24's account of a pre-screening NDA, which the studio says was a standard spoiler agreement; he says it would have required him to sign away rights to his name and image. The trailer has drawn 43 million YouTube views, A24's second-highest ever. "Primetime" opens September 25.
Why This Matters
A24 built "Primetime's" highest-engagement marketing on Chris Hansen's name and story without his cooperation, and that same engagement is now the evidence Hansen points to for what the name was worth to license. That symmetry is new: a biopic's own marketing metrics didn't used to hand the subject a public leverage case before the release date. It resets the opening position for anyone negotiating life rights on a project like this, since the campaign's performance becomes part of the value argument.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting a preview NDA for a subject of a based-on-real-events project should specify precisely which rights it does and doesn't affect. The ambiguity itself became A24's story instead of the film's own marketing.
The Facts
  • Chris Hansen told radio host Dan Abrams on "The Dan Abrams Show" (Wednesday) he hasn't decided whether to pursue legal action against A24's "Primetime." He said an entertainment lawyer told him "you probably have a decent case."
  • "Primetime," directed by Lance Oppenheim and written by Ajon Singh, stars Robert Pattinson as Hansen and adapts Luke Dittrich's Esquire article about a "To Catch a Predator" sting that ended in the suicide of assistant district attorney Bill Conradt after a SWAT raid.
  • The trailer has drawn 43 million views on A24's YouTube channel, the studio's second-most-watched trailer ever, behind "Backrooms."
  • Hansen says A24 required him to sign an NDA before a preview screening that would "sign away my rights to my name, image and brand." A source told The Wrap it was a standard spoiler/IP-protection NDA required of all preview audiences, not a rights waiver.
  • Hansen contrasts his own experience with David Osit, director of the documentary "Predators" about Hansen, who saw "Primetime" without signing such an NDA.
  • A24 declined to comment. "Primetime" opens in theaters September 25.

U.K. Producers Say Streamer Deals Cost Them the IP Rights Public Broadcasters Must Grant
Three top U.K. producers told Puck's Matthew Belloni that streamer commissions leave them no rights retention, while BBC and Channel 4 deals must grant producers the IP in their programs.
CEO Summary
Belloni convened three senior U.K. producers at the Edinburgh TV Festival on Wednesday: Banijay U.K. CEO Patrick Holland, Nutopia CEO Jane Root, and Raw chief creative officer Dimitri Doganis. Under the U.K.'s Terms of Trade, set by the 2003 Broadcasting Act, the BBC and Channel 4 must grant independent producers the IP rights to their programs. The U.K. arms of Netflix and Amazon carry no such requirement. Doganis said producers who take those commissions work for hire and start from zero each year unless they have a returning series.
Why This Matters
Holland said the Banijay and All3Media merger gives him scale he has not yet used against the streamers: "The gun hasn't come out of the holster yet." That is supply-side consolidation held as unspent leverage on rights terms rather than spent on price. Doganis named the same lever more plainly, saying the only real leverage producers have is holding something a buyer wants. Neither said it has worked yet. The $1.2 million to $1.5 million ceiling Doganis put on Netflix true crime commissions suggests the buyer side is not pricing that leverage in.
Specific Implication
Representatives structuring star-led unscripted projects should test whether a YouTube-first launch preserves ownership that a streamer commission would extinguish.
The Facts
  • The panel: Patrick Holland (executive chair and CEO, Banijay U.K.; MasterChef, Big Brother), Jane Root (founder and CEO, Nutopia; Limitless With Chris Hemsworth, WWII With Tom Hanks), Dimitri Doganis (founder and chief creative officer, Raw; The Tinder Swindler, Trainwreck).
  • Belloni framed the stakes: the choice "could be worth billions of dollars to big production companies, which increasingly rely on the global exploitation of I.P. they own."
  • Holland said MasterChef, which started on the BBC, is now made in 70 territories and grew into "this huge I.P.-monetization machine" because the Broadcasting Act gave producers "skin in the game."
  • Editorial note in the piece: Netflix has said it buys U.K. programming almost exclusively from outside producers and offers deals on the U.K. model, but producers overwhelmingly choose buyouts upfront.
  • Doganis said Raw does not own a piece of the top-performing documentaries it makes for Netflix, calling that "an endless source of both pride and pain."
  • On Netflix's price for a true crime documentary, Doganis: "I would say they don't want to spend more than $1.2 million to $1.5 million, and they sometimes will, but they prefer less."
  • Doganis said the sports-documentary market "is definitely not as strong," with streamers moving into live sports instead because sports docs have diminishing returns.
  • Asked whether the All3Media merger lets Banijay demand a model change from Amazon, Netflix and Apple, Holland said: "The gun hasn't come out of the holster yet."
  • Doganis on producer leverage: make the business case that streamers are "sleeping on money" in dormant library titles, or "I've got something you really want, and you're not getting it unless..." He called the second "the only real leverage we have."
  • Root said Nutopia is making shows directly for YouTube and TikTok with Will Smith, Trevor Noah and Jeff Goldblum, brand-funded and owned jointly with the stars, with secondary sales to follow: "We'd own it with Trevor."
  • Doganis cited independently financed projects sold after completion (100 Foot Wave) and equity partners such as Fifth Season and Wiip as a route outside the work-for-hire model.
  • TV fees to the BBC and other public service broadcasters are declining, and the BBC's royal charter is up in 2027.
  • Disclosure carried in the piece: RedBird Capital, an investor in Banijay, is also an investor in Puck.

Tony Romo Is Talking to CBS Sports About Next Steps as New Citations Land
Tony Romo's representative said the CBS Sports lead NFL analyst is discussing next steps with the network, five weeks into the leave that followed his July arrest in Milwaukee.
CEO Summary
CBS Sports placed Romo on leave in late July after his arrest on suspicion of operating while intoxicated. He now faces three citations: first-offense OWI, unsafe passing on the right, and possessing open intoxicants in a vehicle. His spokesperson told TMZ that Romo "accepts full responsibility" and is "communicating with CBS about next steps." A CBS Sports representative did not respond to TheWrap's request for comment.
Why This Matters
CBS Sports chief David Berson framed the pending decision around brand rather than the legal outcome, saying the network has to "consider the impact on our image and our brand." Under Wisconsin law a first-offense OWI is a civil matter, so closing the case will not answer the question Berson actually posed.
The Facts
  • Romo was arrested July 23 by the Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office after deputies stopped his vehicle on Interstate 43, on suspicion of operating while intoxicated, plus an open-container violation and unsafe passing.
  • Under Wisconsin law, a first-offense OWI is generally treated as a civil offense rather than a criminal charge.
  • CBS Sports said at the end of July: "Tony Romo is on leave from his role at CBS Sports until further notice."
  • Romo's spokesperson said they are "working with local authorities to bring this matter to a close" and "communicating with CBS about next steps."
  • The network tapped J.J. Watt to join Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson during Romo's absence.
  • Berson said earlier this month at the network's annual NFL season preview event in New York: "It's an evolving situation, and therefore we're still investigating. There is no timetable or final decision at this time."
  • Berson added: "We have to consider the impact on our image and our brand. That's very important to us." He said the network has "a very deep bench."
